subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF UNITED STATES ARMAMENTS ON ALASKA HIGHWAY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my motion under Standing Order 43 is in regard to an incident which occurred yesterday near Mile 475 on the Alaska Highway in northeastern British Columbia, involving a civilian commercial transport vehicle carrying United States Air Force bombs of the type M20 Rockeye. The vehicle overturned dislodging and spilling a number of these active projectiles over a wide area.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police out of Fort Nelson, who were called to the scene, ordered the closure of the highway, and later in the day a United States military task force, including an explosive ordinance disposal team, arrived via Hercules aircraft at Fort Nelson, British Columbia, to take charge of the material. Having regard to the fact that this shipment was made-and the highly critical clean-up operation commenced-without the involvement or even the knowledge of our own military authorities, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain):
That the Minister of National Defence be required to avail himself of the earliest opportunity to inform the House what action he is contemplating to implement or improve any regulations governing such movements of dangerous military hardware through our country by our NORAD partners.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF LANDINGS IN NORMANDY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter 1 wish to raise is urgent as this is the last day I can do so this year in this chamber. It is important because the event, even though 38 years ago, led to the overthrow of the Hitlerian
Fortress Europe by the western allies of which, at that time, Canada was the third principal force. Mr. Speaker, on June 6,
1944,	allied forces stormed the beaches of Normandy, France, ultimately to achieve, 11 months later, VE Day on May 13,
1945.	In that heroic struggle hundreds of thousands of Canadians participated, soldiers, airmen, sailors-not all men, since there were thousands of women in uniform in World War II.
It would be invidious to pick out units or formations for fear of missing out many brave men, whether soldiers storming the beaches, sailors manning the ships and boats of those first armadas, or the thousands of Canadian airmen who kept the skies relatively clear of the enemy or who prevented the movement of enemy reinforcements.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. Minister of National Defence who, like myself, saw the June 6 landings as the first of the rescue mission to those of us who were on the wrong side of the battle lines by reason of earlier activity:
That this House go on record as saluting the bravery and sacrifice of those Canadians who on June 6, 1944, gave of their lives in the struggle to defeat the evils of Hitlerism and its heartfelt congratulations to those Canadians who survived to go on to ultimate victory.

COST OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND ELECTRICITY-USE OF DAIRY HEATERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, electricity on Prince Edward Island is generated by oil-fired boilers causing that province to have one of the highest electricity rates in Canada. The majority of dairy farmers on P.E.I. use electrical hot water heaters for heating the water used for washing their milking equipment. There are heat exchangers on the market which dairy farmers could use to utilize heat from milk being cooled, to heat the water necessary for washing their equipment. Regular use of these heat exchangers would help to make eastern Canada less dependent on expensive foreign oil. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources immediately change the Canada Oil Substitution Program so that it will include heat exchangers that are available to dairy farmers to utilize the heat from milk to heat water.

subsubtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Acting Prime Minister, in the absence of the Minister of Finance and of the Prime Minister. This week the Government of Canada had to defend the Canadian dollar by running down its foreign exchange
reserves, by borrowing abroad, and by increasing the rate of the Bank of Canada and interest rates generally. If the Canadian dollar is so strong, why must it be defended by higher interest rates which are causing businesses to collapse at near depression lows, and are costing thousands of Canadians their jobs?

subsubtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only say what is obvious, that there is a major problem of confidence in the world today. The meeting at Versailles should-and we all pray that it will-bring about a good amount of confidence in the economy. Canada is reacting to the situation in the same way as the United Kingdom, Germany, and France. We are all looking for ways and means to get out of a very, very difficult international situation.
The Minister of Finance has repeatedly said what was at the roots of the problem. He indicated that fact that the inflation in the United States has gone down to 6 per cent or 7 per cent and the fact that interest rates remain at 16 per cent have created a U.S. dollar attractiveness in the world which is upsetting the world economy at this time.
The other day the Minister of Finance repeated that he would adjust to circumstances. He kept all his options open. He promised to the House that he would review the situation after his return from Versailles. He said that if he had to go to the market for more money, he would present his case to the finance committee and would indicate what were the figures. That is the situation in which we are now, and hopefully by next week, when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance return, we will have a better view of the next steps.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Acting Prime Minister. I should like to correct him. The major problem is not lack of confidence in the international economy; it is lack of confidence in the way the government is running this economy. The government-and the Acting Prime Minister has just repeated this-has repeatedly blamed Canada's economic problems on American economic policy. If that is the case, why are United States interest rates and inflation rates coming down, while Canadian interest rates and inflation rates are continuing to be very high?

Mr. Speaker, I was not very original. I stated the position which is understood to be the one in all countries of the world. The United Kingdom, France and Germany also identify the source of major discomfort in the world today as being the situation which exists, as I explained, in the United States.
My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and myself have indicated a number of things that the opposition could do in a positive fashion to help us all in this situation. I think the opposition has some responsibility also. I
June 4, 1982

mentioned the ports bill as being very important. The hon. member, who comes from the great city of Vancouver, knows that the marine community in Vancouver wants this bill. Why does she not come out now and arrange things so that this bill will be passed? It will create a great amount of enthusiasm in Vancouver about the future of ports and transportation in that city. The members of the opposition, I repeat, have some responsibility also.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF NEW BUDGET
REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF NEW BUDGET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister as well. Since last fall's budget, unemployment in Canada has continued to rise month after month. Today it has reached, in real numbers, almost two million Canadians. Every Canadian knows someone in our country who is unemployed. My question is straightforward. Will the government now acknowledge that its budget is completely out of date, and will it accept its responsibility to provide some job security to Canadians for the coming summer and say that it will bring in a budget before we recess, a budget that recognizes the need for action?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF NEW BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously I cannot answer that question except by repeating what we all said here this morning. The Minister of Employment and Immigration said in particular that a number of programs have been created to take care of chronic unemployment as well as structural unemployment. I will not repeat them all. He has reported in the past few days on a number of programs such as job sharing, and a number of initiatives to help students through the summer. All these things have been done.
There is hope that the meeting at Versailles-1 underline "hope"-might begin to resolve some of the more basic issues in the world today. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance went there, and they said repeatedly before they left that what will come out of Versailles will influence their decisions in the future. That is all I can really say. The hon. member cannot expect me to say more than that today.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF NEW BUDGET
speechtext: The minister should know, as all Canadians know, that the programs that the government has produced up to this point are simply not working. Something in addition is required, and that is the message we are trying to get through to the government.

Mr. Speaker, Canada faces an economic crisis the likes of which we have not seen since the war. What is required now is economic leadership by a government that will level with the people of Canada and make it clear that there are no quick fixes, but will produce some grounds for hope. In this context my supplementary question is for the Acting Prime Minister. Since he and his colleagues refuse to commit themselves to produce a budget before the recess, I would at least ask him if the government
Oral Questions
will recognize that the way we can get job security is to put investment into the manufacturing sector, and at least commit the government to produce some new initiatives to create manufacturing jobs before we recess.

Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member is saying is that what is needed is more government spending. Most people, if not all, agree that one of the causes of inflation in Canada today is the deficit in government expenditures. Most people say that the deficit accumulated by this government is excessive.
My hon. friend has recently discovered that manufacturing will be the solution to Canadian economic problems. At other times in the past others have said that natural resources would be the solution. At other times maybe a few NDPers have said that services were the key to prosperity. My friend loves to go to the west coast. At Prince Rupert three quarters of a billion dollars are being invested in that port. If he goes to Roberts Bank he will find that we are quadrupling the facilities at that port. In Vancouver, container terminals have been expanded.
Order.

I am just repeating this to help hon. members in the House and the population to realize the extent of what the government does now. My hon. friend would like us to do more. That is a debatable argument because, if we did much more, we would contribute to the deficit which contributes to inflation.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, what the minister has said would be humorous if it were not so sad. June 4, 1982

economic leadership and that, in short, it has lost any sense of mandate to govern, and should resign.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, before the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance left, they indicated that, upon their return with the assessment they will be able to make of the world situation following the meeting at Versailles, they will be in a position to review the situation. What I was trying to argue with my hon. friend is on the sort of mood that he tries to create that the Government of Canada is not doing anything. subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF UNITED STATES ARMAMENTS ON ALASKA HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence, of which I have given him notice. It is with regard to the incident which occurred yesterday in northeastern British Columbia, at Mile 375 on the Alaska Highway, involving a civilian commercial transport vehicle carrying dangerous military hardware, namely, United States Air Force bombs of the type M-20 Rockeye. The vehicle overturned, spilling a number of these bombs over a wide area. Incredibly, no one was on site to inform the public of the hazards associated with this incident,
nor was our military authority nor the minister's office informed of the shipment.
First of all, it was done without consent. The clean-up operation, involving a United States military team which arrived in Fort Nelson in a Hercules aircraft, was also carried out without the knowledge and consent of our own military authorities. I would like to ask the minister whether he is prepared, after the question period, to make a statement with regard to this important and serious incident?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF UNITED STATES ARMAMENTS ON ALASKA HIGHWAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have the details here of the accident to which the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River has referred. I will supply him with some of the details of this accident, if he wants them, but I do not think there is any need to make a statement on this issue. The involvement of the Department of National Defence is only marginal. It was routine shipment of munitions from Alaska to the United States, which happens quite often. All precautions were taken. The shipment was passed through customs, the necessary permit was obtained from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and everything which had to be done was done. All the munitions were properly crated and rendered what we call "safe", so they could not explode.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF UNITED STATES ARMAMENTS ON ALASKA HIGHWAY
speechtext: What else could they do?

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF UNITED STATES ARMAMENTS ON ALASKA HIGHWAY
speechtext: 1 repeat, all precautions were taken to ensure that there could be no accident. The accident was probably caused by the driver. I do not know exactly how it happened, but as far as the public in the area is concerned, there was no risk to life, risk of explosion or anything like that. The clean-up is under the control of the emergency people from Alaska and from the company, and the Alaska Highway will be opened in due course.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF UNITED STATES ARMAMENTS ON ALASKA HIGHWAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the answer is sufficient.

subtopic: CLOSING OF HIGHWAY TO CIVILIAN TRAFFIC
CLOSING OF HIGHWAY TO CIVILIAN TRAFFIC
speechtext:
The fact is that this shipment was made under permit from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It was not a specific permit, but one which covers all such shipments on an annual basis. The fact is that the military authorities who were asked about the danger instructed the RCMP to close the highway. The highway has been closed to civilian traffic for a day. These bombs are loaded. They were equipped with safety pins, yes, but I am told by the military officials that if a train had hit the truck, say, near the metropolitan centre of Vancouver, these bombs may well have exploded.
It is incredible that our military authorities are not informed of these shipments. I am not denying that these shipments have to be made. Certainly under our arrangements with NORAD, our air space and our highways will from time to time be exposed to these dangers. We should certainly be prepared to
June 4, 1982

accept these dangers, but there must surely be more control. We must be informed so that, when an incident occurs, the public can be informed of the danger and hazards associated with it, and civilian transportation facilities can be kept in place.
1 ask the minister again, will he first of all order his officials to review the procedures governing such shipments? And, at the earliest opportunity, will he make a statement in the House on the outcome of such a review and what he intends to do to allay some of the obvious fears that the people in my constituency presently have concerning the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CLOSING OF HIGHWAY TO CIVILIAN TRAFFIC

speechtext:

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation with young people in this country is one that is now being shared across the economy. There is a lack of growth in the economy. This is something that is being shared by all industrial countries. We have tried to put a program in place that will supply work for over

Again, we are dealing with a situation and circumstance which is shared by all countries, as we have seen in the discussions as a prelude to the Summit meeting. Mr. Speaker, the last point in particular regarding the treatment of foreign investment in Canada is debatable. In a debate on that subject, different positions are taken. This morning I tried to indicate to the opposition that a number of things can be done which necessitate their support. I was quite blunt about it. There are a number of instances in which they could be helpful in restoring confidence. Occasionally the opposition should do something other than oppose.
I might mention that this morning great emphasis was placed on the unemployment figures. Another stack of figures came out this morning. No one has mentioned them yet. Yesterday I read an article from Paris "Match" which stated that, of five leading countries, Canada is considered the place with the highest standard and the place which inspires most confidence. It is about time that we reimported that confidence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my leader who is unavoidably absent, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the crisis in the Canadian economy, composed of the following disturbing elements: the record high level of unemployment of 10.2 per cent of the work force, nearly two million Canadians if the hidden unemployed are included; the collapse of the National Energy Program; the weakening of the Canadian dollar; and the increase in Canadian interst rates. All of these elements constitute an economic national emergency unprecedented in the post-war period requiring immediate action to put into place a program of national economic regeneration.

June 4, 1982

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY ALLEGED NATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
As provided for in Section (2) of Standing Order 26, the hon. member for Oshawa has given me due notice of his intention to move the adjournment of the House to discuss the crisis in the Canadian economy.
There can be no doubt as to the importance of this subject for all members of the House. The application refers to problems which have been of concern to the House and various aspects of this chronic and continuing problem have been discussed almost on a daily basis for an extended period of time.
A series of bills relating to the National Energy Program have been and will be discussed by the House for weeks. speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-115, to establish a national program for occupational training, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as we discussed during question period this morning, members of this House are quite justifiably concerned about the level of unemployment in this country and are asking for some real answers on that issue.
National Training Act
How can we come to grips with the problems facing many Canadians without jobs? Mr. Speaker, today members of this House have the opportunity to do something very real, tangible and concrete about that problem. We are introducing for second reading a bill which will authorize the government to put in place a brand new national training program, one that will affect young people, workers in existing plants and factories, and those coming into the work force. The bill will affect literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are attempting to respond to changing economic conditions. So, Mr. Speaker, in a very immediate sense there is an opportunity for this House to show Canadians that we are concerned, not just in a rhetorical way, but in a very clear and real way, and that this Parliament can take action to respond to their needs.
Equally important is the fact that this bill will provide a foundation and framework for developing responses to the job market throughout the 1980s. We will be experiencing major alterations in the way people work in Canada. There will be a new world of work, a new technology and new industry which will require a substantially different set of skills on the part of Canadians. There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that one of the most important investments we can make as a government is to ensure Canadians are capable of responding to this new technology with the appropriate skills.

In the '80s we are going to see a number of changes; changes in the price of energy, in our industries, in computer science and in technology. Workers will have to adapt to these changes. Mobility, re-training and new work standards are aspects that will become more important for Canadian workers. For instance, there will be more women in the labour market. Training and education will be necessary to fill the positions that will be developed during the '80s. The job world is changing.

Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I addressed a conference of combined representatives of community colleges across Canada, the people who provide a large proportion of this training. The conference dealt with the impact of new technology. They realize that in a very few years there will be major adjustments for people working in the service industries, such as insurance companies, banks and the public service. Secretarial pools will be replaced by word processors. Of course, this raises, honestly so, the fear over the impact this new technology will have, and whether it will put people out of work. Mr. Speaker, I do not fully associate myself with those concerns because I believe new technology also creates work, but only if people are trained for and able to adapt to the new skills required. So we are talking about an investment in the future of this country of immense proportions. We are talking about assuring hundreds of thousands of Canadians that they have hope in the future.

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
It is important to note as an historical footnote that the introduction of this training act is one of the first clear examples of the way in which the parliamentary task forces, established two years ago, have been able to have a major impact on government policy. Members will recall that at the beginning of the new Parliament the government established five or six task forces to enable it to come to grips with changes in the economy and society. One of the most important of those was the task force chaired by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), but with a membership from all three parties. That task force visited communities right across Canada and met with all kinds of Canadians in business, labour and education. A very clear message came from those Canadians that we needed changes in our training programs. We needed more money, new institutions, and we needed to improve substantially our flexibility in order to produce a first-class training system, one of the best in the world. I want to say to Members of Parliament, particularly those on that committee who spent many long hours working on the report, that they can see in this bill a very clear reflection of their investment of time, energy and creativity in that task force.
This government has honoured their work by bringing forward a new training bill which will give us the opportunity to establish the foundations of a new training system in Canada. I wanted to pay my own compliments, Mr. Speaker, to the members of that task force for the work they have undertaken. Equally so to those members of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, with whom it has been my great delight and pleasure to meet on many occasions during the two years I have been the minister of this department. On those occasions they provided a number of new and creative suggestions as to how we should deal with training in Canada. Again, this bill is a reflection of their contribution.
The bill is not something which is necessarily the subject of partisan debate; it is something we can all agree to and should agree to because it reflects a sharing of responsibility of members from all parties. That is what gives me particular pleasure in being able to bring forward this bill. However, I want to provide one caution, Mr. Speaker. I do so with a clear realization that Members of Parliament will want to have the opportunity to debate this bill and to discuss its merits and suggest whatever kinds of amendments or concerns they might have.
I would put toward them a very clear choice. We can either spend a long time going over territory that we have gone over before and thereby run the risk of having this bill sit on the agenda for months on end, or perhaps even lose the bill because at the close of the summer session it may die on the Order Paper; or we can enact this bill with dispatch so that it can become law and we can get down to the business of training Canadians in a new kind of way.
I make a special appeal to members of this House, in particular in this debate today on second reading, to allow us
to have second reading today so that the bill can go to committee. Then we can spend time in committee going over the details. If we are not given the opportunity to pass the bill on second reading, with the kind of parliamentary timetable and agenda that we are facing we are running the risk of not having this bill proceed further. I particularly address my remarks to the members of the opposition to help them realize that the choice is in their hands. With the kind of demand they were making today in question period, a legitimate demand, that this government do something to help Canadians and especially young Canadians, it is very clearly their responsibility. We can do something very real today by giving this bill passage and moving it through committee so that it will become the law of the land and we can get on with the training of Canadians.
Why is it so important, Mr. Speaker? Let me spend a moment giving a short history to show why this bill is central to the initiation and development of a new training system for Canadians. The Allmand task force, a task force that was commissioned by my own department, clearly showed that there were major faults in the present system. Perhaps the most important omission was that our present training system, largely funded by the federal government to the tune of over $800 million in the past year, was training a number of people for jobs that were not there, jobs that no longer existed. In some regions of the country over 30 per cent of those enrolling in the training programs supported under the Adult Occupational Training Act were in surplus occupations. That engendered enormous frustration on the part of the people who enrolled in those programs. It simply meant that we were not making good use of the money that was being expended in large sums in an effort to help Canadians get these new skills.
The recommendation that we have received is to develop a program that will target our training dollars towards those occupations which are in demand, to put the money where the jobs will be, to ensure that at the end of the training program there will be employment. This legislation is the keystone of that recommendation.
We were also told, Mr. Speaker, that it was very important, before we went forward with legislation, to have very close and open consultation, so that not only would we take the recommendations of the task force but we would also have two federal-provincial conferences on the issue of training; that we would present a basic policy framework to provincial ministers, sharing in the responsibility, so that they would have the opportunity to react.
The national training program that we put forward last January contained the following elements. First, that we have to improve substantially the planning of manpower and labour market programs. We need much better information than we now have. Although we were in a modern technology society, we were flying blind in terms of assessing needs. We did some at the federal level and some at the provincial manpower commission level, some of the schools did some, but it was fragmentary; no one integrated the information.
We are proposing to develop what we call an occupational protective system. Under that system we will take the best information that can be gathered at the federal level, the
June 4, 1982

statistics that we have, and the kind of information we develop in terms of a national labour market, and combine and integrate that with the information obtained by provincial governments and manpower commissions and departments of colleges and universities. We would also integrate that with private industry information so that we can get a real assessment as to what industry requirements sector by sector will be.
To that end, over the past year we have been signing a number of employment agreements with different industrial sectors. We have signed agreements with the mining associations, with aerospace, with the graphics industry, with the foundries industry. We can begin to put in place a network of arrangements across the country with private industry so that we can share information, and when we have that information we can identify where the shortfall may be, where the problems may be and target our resources.
Therefore, one of the key elements in the new national training program is a national program of information development and planning, so that we have a clear ability-not perfect but certainly an improvement on what we have now- to plan where we want to go. And what about an information pool, a reservoir of information? We will be in a position to begin designating priority occupations in consultation with provincial governments and private industry. By priority occupations we do not mean just those that are in demand on the national level. We mean those which also have regional and local requirements. That means that we will be able to target our resources in training to those occupations where there is a need, so that our training programs will have a direct relationship to the job market. We need the authority to do that, Mr. Speaker. That is one of the key ingredients and elements in this bill. It will give us authority to begin providing those designated occupations so that federal dollars going into the training system will be allocated to wherever the demand may be.
We also recognize that if we are to make major changes in the training system, adjustments will have to be made, changes will have to be brought about. In particular, there will have to be a substantial modernization of training facilities. I have visited many of our community colleges and plants and factories. I found to my horror that sometimes people are training on equipment that is 30 or 40 years out of date. They simply do not have up-to-date facilities. They know that we are moving into a new era of information technology, yet many of our schools and training systems simply do not have a computer terminal.
Let me give an example from a visit I made a few weeks ago to the marine college on Prince Edward Island. One of the anomalies or paradoxes we face is that, in a growing industry on the east coast of Canada, the offshore oil and gas industry, we are having to recruit workers from offshore because there are not enough trained marine engineers or navigators to supply the needs of those industries. Yet we have a college, a good college, on Prince Edward Island that is training people for those occupations, but they are working on navigational machinery which was built during the Second World War. They say: "We need a new computer, a new simulator, and we
National Training Act
can turn out an additional hundred marine engineers a year to supply the industry". So for lack of one piece of equipment, we are denying a high-skilled, high-technology job to 100 Canadians per year.
At the same time we realize that there are enormous demands for expansion of training facilities. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) knows that in Toronto there was a report just last week that Seneca College has received over
15,000	applications from people for their high-technology training school and they have places for only 8,000. Seneca College now has applications in front of us and the provincial government of Ontario for expansion of that program.
This legislation authorizes the Government of Canada to go into a new program called the skills growth fund. It will provide direct grants to training centres and institutions across Canada for the expansion and modernization of facilities.

speechtext:
Whatever the reason, I am not going to lay the blame. I simply say that if we are going to bring about a new system of training we have to recognize that we will need a new curriculum, new courses. We will have to retrain many of our faculty members, provide new equipment and new facilities. Mr. Speaker, we have put $108 million this year on the line to be spent, and we could be spending it the very moment this legislation is passed. Those 15,000 applicants for Seneca College in Toronto could be going to school next fall if we get the legislation passed now. They could be in the new training classes. But we need the money to do it, and this is why we need to have this bill passed right away. We cannot pass it if we are not given authority by Members of Parliament to spend the money. It is not a matter of budget. We have increased the training budget by 15 per cent this year to over $1 billion, but under the laws of the land I cannot spend it unless I have the authority of Parliament. This is why we are here today, asking for authority to modernize substantially the system of training for all Canadians.
Equally important is the question of the kind of training. In this respect I should like to turn to some of the recommendations of the Allmand task force which we took into account. Not only should we be training in high technology jobs, as critical as that may be; we must begin to tackle the problem of the hard core unemployed, such as young persons, drop-outs and persons who do not get a chance and for reasons of lack of education or skills are always on the sidelines in the job market.
We have carefully analysed the problem of youth unemployment. Something close to 200,000 young people in the country are on what we call the margin of society. They are the people who drop out of school at grade seven or grade eight. They may obtain jobs for a couple of months washing dishes, but generally they are in and out of the job market. They are virtually the transients of the job market. We believe we can tackle that problem, come to grips with the structurally

National Training Act
unemployed and give those people a chance through the introduction of training programs.
Up to this point in time, the Adult Occupational Training Act has provided major deterrents to doing this because of certain age requirements. This bill contains a fundamental change in the flexibility which we can offer to young Canadians, because we are changing the definition of who is eligible for training under the act. I draw the attention of hon. members to the definition of "adult" under the old act as someone who was one year beyond the school system. We are now defining an adult as any person which the school system says is of a school-leaving age. This means that we can now open up training to those who drop out of school at grades seven and eight.
The hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) has offered suggestions on more than one occasion that we must do this. This bill responds to that responsibility. I also draw this to the attention of hon. members from western Canada where there is a problem with high unemployment among native people. We know that something like 70 per cent of young natives leave school before graduation. Under this program we would be able to begin developing training programs for these people to provide them with new skills and opportunities to obtain jobs and, therefore, they could take advantage of the changes in the marketplace.
In addition, we are talking in this bill about recognizing the changing labour market by providing the ability to waive the requirement that training only be offered for 52 weeks. This is in recognition of the fact that many training programs, particularly in the high skills area, extend beyond the normal 52-week period. The bill authorizes my commission to waive that responsibility, and where training is to be provided beyond 52 weeks, we can again provide funding. Equally, we can now provide new funding for Canadians not only in traditional or conventional training centres but for those in new kinds of consortiums or arrangements put together by employers. Rather than agreeing to supply training for one employer, which we found tended to discriminate against the smaller business person with a small shop employing only 40 or 50 people which would not want to commence a program on their own, we are authorizing an arrangement whereby small employers can come together, either through a union or an employers' association, to initiate a joint training program. This means that one employer might provide training for machinists, another for heavy duty mechanics, and another for pipefitters, for example. This would mean that small factories in manufacturing areas would be able to become involved in a training consortium.
Also there is provision under the bill whereby we would provide direct training for certain special groups that want to provide training in new skills for people in society with special needs. This would be beneficial to organizations such as the Gabriel Dumont Centre in Saskatchewan which is operated by non-status natives who want to get into training programs which are related to their own needs. Under the program we
would be able to provide training assistance under the industrial training program for such people. It will substantially expand the flexibility of our training system to provide new kinds of training facilities, new polytechnics, new etudes, new centres and new institutes which were previously difficult to form under the national training program. We have broadened the range of training facilities.
Also the bill will enable the federal government to develop new financial arrangements with the provinces to eliminate much of the red tape and the administrative regulatory handicaps which were there before. For example, previously in the training system we would have purchased courses from a provincial institute. This required very detailed record keeping to ensure that the course was administered and that people attended the course, and the provinces had to submit their bills at the end of the year. Under this new arrangement we have the alternative of engaging in a flat rate formula with the provinces, so that we can eliminate red tape, provide for the purchase of courses and the sharing of administrative costs on a direct fee basis. This recommendation was strongly suggested to us by provincial governments.
We have attempted in this bill to respond to a number of concerns. I should like to talk for a moment about some of the ongoing misconceptions about these areas. First, let me talk about the grand, old perennial Canadian problem called "money". Members of Parliament have asked many times what commitment the government is making to future employment for Canadians. As 1 indicated, we are making a commitment this year of over $1 billion, which is well over a 15 per cent increase over last year. The money is allocated to our reserve to be spent the moment the bill is passed. We have made a commitment, and we can provide for the alternatives which many hon. members of the House have requested.
A second misconception concerns jurisdiction and the suggestions that at times there are problems relating to who will deliver the program or whether it is really an intrusion of the federal government into provincial jurisdiction. The fact of the matter is that we are again doing what hon. members have requested, that is, ensuring accountability for federal money which is spent to ensure that we will spend the money according to the needs and demands of the national marketplace, but not in any arbitrary or unilateral way.
The entire thesis of this bill and our training program is to consult with the provinces and private industry, to develop priority occupations based upon those consultations, to work jointly and to share responsibility, but still to maintain accountability at the federal level for the money we spend. We are not intruding; we are simply engaging in a more wholesome partnership where obviously as a federal government we must share responsibility with provincial institutions, the private sector and labour unions. Under this bill we will be able to begin to enact that kind of shared responsibility and to provide for a combination and a partnership in the training of Canadians. I hope hon. members will not be deluded by those tangential arguments which we often hear because people are


June 4, 1982

more interested at times in creating mischief, disruption and confrontation than in trying to create something which is positive and will work.
This legislation is not written in stone. It can go to committee, we are prepared to look at amendments there and to respond to the preoccupations of hon. members. We are also prepared to consider that this is simply a foundation or a base upon which we can then build the training program. We do not say that it has all the answers, but we are talking about the beginning of a new system. We see the need for substantial new retraining programs across the country which we can provide under the bill. We see the need for new co-op education programs so that we can provide much closer arrangements between industries and schools. We see the need for major changes in adult retraining so that when the adult population faces the need to change jobs or their occupation they can begin to develop programs either through the community college, their union or their employer. A new training act is necessary to bring that about. We need a new training act that is based upon the operation of basic principles that allow the federal government to operate through the medium of a national labour market and which would also ensure that we can target our resources and modernize the system. That is the purpose and direction of this bill.
I strongly recommend this legislation to members of the House. Again, I reiterate that it is my sincere hope that members will recognize how much responsibility we have on this Friday afternoon. Friday afternoon is not usually a time that is used to make great advances in Parliament. Most members find it convenient to return to their ridings on Friday afternoon. I would say, however, that we have an opportunity today to do something very important and significant for Canadians. By giving this bill second reading we will launch the means for the initiation of a new training plan for Canadians which will ensure them the opportunity to meet the future working world.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that I am pleased to participate in this debate today. I would like to underline the minister's last comment. I also believe that this is not simply a minor event which is occurring during the longest session of Parliament's history. I have reviewed all the legislation which we have dealt with in the House, including the budget statement, the National Energy Program and the Constitution debate. If I had to choose a piece of legislation which will or ought to have a greater impact on Canadians in the next 20 years, it is this piece of legislation.
No member of the House should underestimate the significance of the bill which is before us. Its importance should not simply be considered for what it will achieve in the next year or two, but indeed in the next 20 years. After reading the bill and the available literature, and after engaging in discussions with people, I was astonished by how little most of the people
National Training Act
to whom I talked knew about the history of technical, technological and vocational education in this country and, indeed, the history of the federal government's role in these areas. I thought I might spend some time on that history for the benefit of those who have not had the opportunity to look at it.
I think it will be instructive not only to ourselves but also to the government and others who may be interested.
The principles in the bill which we are discussing today on second reading are not new. They are an extension of certain principles developed in the past but they are not of themselves new. It is perhaps a type of arrogance of any current generation which makes it believe that everything it does is brand new. That is why I think the historical record is instructive.
It comes as no surprise to anyone in the House that education was given to the provinces in 1867. Interestingly enough, it was within eight or ten years-by 1876-that the federal government took its first step into the field of education. What is equally interesting is that this first step occurred in the minister's home province of Manitoba where the federal government provided lands for the development of an institution which would one day become the University of Manitoba. In the same year the federal government began programs for training its own people under RCMP programs.
Almost as soon as confederation was achieved the federal government began to move into the field of education on demand in the sense that there needed to be some involvement from the central government which dealt with matters common to all Canadians.
I will not go through the complete history but there are certain watersheds in the historical development which can be instructive. It was not until 1980 that we decided in our Canadian way to do something about the fact that we had an embarrassment of riches which we discovered when we opened up the west. We found that we had a tremendous amount of natural resources. As the new technology of that age and the new economy at that time began to develop, we realized that there were shortages of skilled people and that there were no programs or funds available to train the young Canadians of the first decade of the twentieth century for future jobs. In 1910 we established a royal commission on industrial training and vocational education. One of the great unusual consequences of that royal commission was that it was one of those royal commissions that was effective. It was actually used and its recommendations were put into law.
Two acts which were spin-offs of that first big watershed in 1910 and flowed out of the recommendations of the royal commission were the agricultural assistance act and the agricultural instruction act. Those spawned the first animal husbandry courses and the first agricultural institutions in western Canada. The National Research Council was established in 1916 as a result of one of the recommendations.
In 1919 the bulwark for the next 20 years of technological education was established. It was the technical education act which lasted from 1919 to 1939. It provided to a generation and a half of Canadians the Financial and institutional base by which it coped with the technology of that generation.

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
In 1942 there was another watershed: the vocational training and co-ordination act was adopted. It was quickly adopted for two reasons; first, the old act had died; and second, we had a new reality in Canada, which was the war. We needed to train people for a host of new technologies coming into the world which were ushered in by the war. Therefore, the vocational training and vocational act of 1942 became the new federal base.
The Veterans Rehabilitation Act of 1945 was established to direct for the first time in any significant way funding by the federal government to students in technical, technological and vocational training.
In 1960 we began the phase which we are presently going through. The Technical and Vocational Training and Assistance Act was established by the Conservative government of John Diefenbaker. I mention this as a watershed along with 1910 and 1942. The 1960 act brought about a major change in the role of the federal government in technical and technological education. In fact, it provided vast quantities of funds for capital development in much the same way as the principle of the minister's bill. It established funds for technical and vocational high schools, not simply for people who were in the high school system but for technical and vocational high schools. This was done in the Atlantic provinces, western Canada and central Canada.
Those who benefited from technical and vocational education in those days were direct beneficiaries of a large infusion of funds, programs and schools as well as the training of teachers by the federal government. For those interested in the extent to which the federal government was involved in technical, technological and vocational training in Canada through the 1960 program, the fact is that the federal government in the short span of seven years established 688 new schools and renovated 440 of those schools from one end of the country to the other.
This brings us up to 1967. A new act called the Adult Occupational Training Act became the base for Canadian manpower training programs which we have enjoyed since that time. The purpose of that act in 1967 is worth quoting. This was an act "designed to contribute to the economic and social development of Canadians while reducing regional and individual disparities and providing employment related training".
Maybe everthing else old is new again and maybe there is nothing new under the sun. The point 1 am making in all of this historical development is that the federal government in Canada has been involved in a long history of training, over 70 years. It has provided billions of dollars, thousands of programs and trained millions of Canadians. Now, I emphasize that because I know there are people who are not aware that this is not a new reality. It is a new time and we have new technologies, but the federal government has always been, at least since 1910, and in my view ought to continue to be, one which plays a leading role in the development of funds, institutions, programs and teachers for technical, technological and vocational education.
That historical development also establishes, I think, certain Canadian ways in which we have gone about the federal role, and there are three principles that I think are worth mentioning. First of all, in 1910, from 1939 to 1942, in 1960 and in 1967, each time that the federal government took another step and participated in the development of technological and vocational education, it did so in relation to clearly understood national, industrial and economic strategies. National technical, technological and vocational training is not something that is stuck in the door all by itself. It is just not a sheaf of paper or a bunch of programs that have no connection with anything else. The motivation each time that this country has taken a leap forward in its economic programs and its industrial strategy has been the adoption of a national training program.
Now, it is important to emphasize that first principle. I wish the government well, but if it is to sell its program, not just to other governments but to the people of this country, then it will have to make its goals more clear than what we have heard so far in terms of national industrial strategies and national economic recovery programs. Because then people will understand the funds and the involvement in provincial policies which will also be required.
Indeed, as the minister himself indicated, we are going into a new world, as we did in 1910, as we did in 1942 and as we did in 1967. We are going into a new world where the speed of change is very great-a world of robots, a world of computers, a technological revolution. I guess that that type of technological revolution was just as scary at the turn of the century, in a sense, but it offered the same opportunities. One thing is clear with the current one. We now live in an integrated world economy where, unless we do have a national industrial strategy of economic recovery and a national training program which fits it, we will not become world competitive.
The second principle usually does not occupy the interest of parliamentarians at the federal level, but it is one worth pointing out because there are parts of the bill which will receive considerable scrutiny in committee, at least from me. It involves the way in which we balance education, in its broadest definition, and technical education. I will not spend much time on it today, but I wish to flag the problem within the bill. I think there is an idea that we must somehow move away from educational institutions, and that if there has been a bias in that direction, we must move away over to the other bias so that we have more and more exclusion of institution and more and more employer-based education.
As any educator would advise, there are a number of philosophies. There is one which suggests that the most important way in which to have technological and vocational education is to have it in the workplace. The extreme opposite is to have it only in the educational institutions. Indeed, we have veered from one to the other. Throughout the western world one will find countries which represent one philosophy more than the other.
What is required, and it certainly fits well in the Canadian mould, is a balance. There must be a balance between the

June 4, 1982

training of people for jobs and the training of people for life. There is no dichotomy in the individual's mind. There is always a dichotomy between levels of government and government bureaucracies. I heard what the minister pointed out in his speech. At least, I hope the minister said what I think I heard him say, because it is a good idea. When people work at whatever they do, they develop their own personalities. Their work tells them who and what they are and who and what they will become. Therefore, when we talk about training, it is wise to ensure that that training takes place within the context of an over-all educational program. I speak not only of philosophy here. If the federal government persists in the view, which I hope it does not, that it can split training from education and therefore split itself from provincial co-operation, it will not only cause a problem between governments, but will also mean that it has not done its work well in serving the people of Canada. It is absolutely essential that that second principle of balance between education and training, between institutions and the work place, be maintained.
I might say that a while ago I spent some time on this matter. For the minister's edification, he might want to speak to the chairman of his advisory committee on immigration, Mr. Tom Sosa, who is vice-president of Ryerson Polytechnical Institute. I have a great love and affection for what I call the Ryerson model. It did not always do the job it was supposed to do, but its model was the best model. I commend it to the minister.
The problem for technological and technical education in the province of Ontario in the fifties and sixties was that the moneys went to the universities and there was nothing for that level of technical and technological education. Up until 1966, there was only one institute in the province of Ontario which carried out that level. That was Ryerson Polytechnical Institute or the old Ryerson Institute of Technology established in 1948. The principle behind the model was that one should link work to the job and link work to education so that it carried out an in-service program at the same time carried out a program within the educational institution. That model, I might say, was broken during the change in educational philosophy across the country in the 1960s. Previously Ryerson had to finance itself on the basis of running a very tight ship, ensuring that its graduates had jobs and that its departments were able to fund the students who were coming in. Cooperation between industry on the one hand and the high schools on the other was what made the Ryerson model work. I commend it to the minister.
The third principle is the principle which makes the other two possible. In my view, the first principle is that the government must make clear its national industrial and economic recovery goals in order to make sense out of a national program of technical education. Second, it must create that balance between the needs of education for individuals and the need for training. Third, it must establish co-operation between the levels of government.
National Training Act
With regard to the minister and, indeed, any minister, it is always easier if one does not have to try to talk to the people who will also be involved with you in the same business. It is simply easier to do it yourself.
I note that the hour is now one o'clock, Mr. Speaker; I would like to continue after the lunch hour.
