speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the lunch break I had commenced my remarks by going through the historical development of technical, technological and vocational education. I had outlined the three significant principles that come from that historical development. In my view, these three principles have served us exceedingly well and will serve us in the future if the government pays attention to them.
The first principle is that any program of national training should be part of a national economic recovery as it was in 1910, 1942, 1960 and 1967. It is important that that principle be understood by the government. Second, the program must be an appropriate balance between the needs of so-called education for life and the needs of technical training, education specifically for the workplace, that a balance be maintained and that we not sacrifice one for the other as has so often been the case at other times and in other places. The third principle, the one I was dealing with when the hour struck one o'clock, is the principle of co-operation.
Throughout each of our watershed periods when the federal government has become involved in a significant way with respect to technical and technological education there has been the requisite, not easy to achieve, co-operation with the provinces. That in my view, particularly with this bill, is a very important principle. As it stands right now, the bill commits the government to consultation but does not commit it to agreement. I recognize some of the difficulties the minister may see, but when we do the questioning during committee stage and report stage, we will be able to develop an argument and the minister will see the value of agreement with the provinces.
To put it in the shortest possible way I can, if the government cannot find agreement with the provinces, we will have lost two things, with disharmony again being on us. First, we will have lost that intricate relationship between education and training. We would have the provincial governments dealing with education and the federal government dealing with training. We will have lost the necessary integration between the two. In short, we will have lost the second principle.
Also, we would have lost the opportunity to develop what is inherent in the principles of this bill, namely the best possible approach that a federal political system can take in terms of

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
the development of training in technical and technological education.
The third principle, that of co-operation between the two levels of government, is essential. Indeed, the other two principles which have served us so well will not be successful unless that co-operation is clear and obvious. The best way to do that is in connection with agreements so that the individual is served by both levels of government rather than having them at war one with the other.
In his speech the other day to the presidents of community colleges from across the country, the minister said at the bottom of page 8 of his speech: "We will invest in new facilities, equipment, curriculum and build the kinds of institutions needed to train Canadians in new skills for new jobs". I support that. I think all Canadians support that. What is important is the definition of "we". "We" should not be the federal government and should not even be the federal Parliament. If it is to be successful, "we" means the federal level, the provincial level, private institutions and those involved in the delivery of education. "We" means all of those who deliver the service, and it also means those who receive that service. It is on the definition of "we" that I think the success or failure of the minister's bill will be determined.
This brings me finally to the specifics of the legislation now before us. As I think I probably have been able to demonstrate, this bill in 1982 is serving the same need Canadians had in 1910, in 1942, in 1960 and again in 1967. We have a system today that has many problems, and I suppose as too often Canadians try to do, we try to point the finger at who caused the problems. Who is to blame? The fact is we are all to blame. The federal government is to blame.
The minister says we have been pouring millions of dollars into training programs for which there are no jobs. Most of those millions of dollars have come from the federal government. The federal government had the opportunity for approval of those programs and, indeed, as the task force on work in the eighties pointed out, the minister's own department wasted-I think that was the word used-millions of dollars training people for no jobs. There clearly is a responsibility at the federal level. The provincial governments have their share too.
The glories of an educational institution being run like a grand corporation caught the imagination of too many people involved in education in the sixties and seventies, and far more money was spent on administrative and on non-teaching and non-learning aspects of technical, technological and vocational education than needed to be. The provinces too often looked for the glory and less for the delivery of the service. However, we as parents were also responsible. Particularly in this field we have for too long-for the last 30 years-assumed that somehow if we were involved in technical, technological or vocational work, that was not quite up to snuff in relation to what people ought to be. We put far too much emphasis on grants to universities and too little on the importance of doing the good, honest work required. We lost the sense of having
pride in good labour done. We lost that in the last generation and a half, and I am hoping one of the things which will come out of this bill will be a recapturing of the understanding of the contribution that technical, technological and vocational jobs make, not just to the economy of the country but, indeed, to society as a whole. Who we blame is not important to the future. I think we are all to blame. The fact is we now have a technical, technological and vocational system that is not serving us.
The specifics of the bill are four in number. First, the minister argues as a question of principle at second reading of the bill that we have to have the identification of priority occupations, and those ought to be the major business of the federal government. I agree with that. That was clearly the principle in 1960. It was also clearly the principle in 1967, in 1942 and in 1910. That is the principle now. It is a good principle. The federal government should be concerned about those priority occupations which will allow us to deal with the technical and technological revolution that is already upon us. Indeed, we should have been concerned about it eight or ten years ago.
Second, the bill argues for a greater opportunity to have employers and non-educational institutions involved in the delivery of technical, technological and vocational training outside institutions. I support that too. I think there are lots of opportunities to use the facilities of those non-educational institutions. To give an example, what is the best marketing school in Canada? Some people might think it is the University of Western Ontario. I think most people would understand it is Procter and Gamble-sorry to Lever Brothers! There is great value in training in the workplace, but not at the cost of education in the institution. The principle is good. We are going to have to wait until the regulations and the agreements show whether that balance between education and training is maintained.
Third, the bill talks about the necessity for projecting employment needs and offers what is known in the trade as COPS, the Canada occupational projection system. It is a computer-based system which allows for some understanding of what we are going to need in the future. I think the minister would admit that it is not terrific, but it is all we have at this point.
What I would like to suggest to the minister, and will be suggesting in the committee, is that he pick up on a suggestion which has been made to him on a number of occasions. He could refine it to his own use, but it is a suggestion with respect to participation by the Canadian Labour Congress and the Business Council on National Issues. It is not very often both labour and management get together with a proposal. They have made a proposal to the minister. It seems to me that even if the specifics of that proposal are not sufficient for the minister and if he would like to use COPS in connection with it, I think the Business Council on National Issues and the Canadian Labour Congress would be happy to listen to some proposals from the minister so that they could participate in labour market projections. We should not simply write labour
June 4, 1982

market projections off as a theoretical system. Being able to project what we will need in terms of skilled talent is a very, very important matter. Otherwise, our ability to be able to organize resources in time and, indeed to be able even to lead the market for a change, would be lost.
Finally, the bill would spend more money both in terms of capital costs and in terms of funds for individuals. Indeed, one measure that I think is excellent would increase benefits to individuals from 60 per cent to 70 per cent and would therefore give people the incentive to get involved in the training programs proposed in the bill.
I can conclude my remarks by saying two things. As I have tried to indicate, this bill has a noble tradition. It is a tradition not known to very many Canadians, but it is a tradition which has served us well, and it has served us well because we have observed those three principles. I implore the minister to pay attention to those principles: national training should be related to national economic recovery; national training should have a balance between the needs of education and the needs of the workplace; and national training should be done within the atmosphere and framework of co-operation and the search for agreement between the two levels of government. If the government does that, I think the name Axworthy will be right up there with the names of those people who piloted the bills through in 1910, in 1942, 1960 and 1967, and that will be well deserved.
However, if the minister fails to pay attention to those principles, he will not only have failed, but we also will have lost the one opportunity we have to become competitive in the world and to be on the road to recovery for the next 20 years.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the unemployment line, the soup kitchen, children attending Salvation Army services not just for spiritual sustenance but for food, are all realities in Canada today. Canadians are in deep trouble. Unemployment is at its highest level since the depression. We are spending some $1 billion on training while skilled jobs go begging. Yet in spite of this situation, things could be different if we had the political will to make them different.
I would like to take a few minutes to describe to hon. members the kind of situation we find ourselves in in Canada today. We have an intolerable level of unemployment. In real terms the number of unemployed is some two million, yet at this time of record levels of unemployment we still have shortages of skilled workers. There are jobs for skilled workers that are not filled by Canadians. This situation is not temporary, although sometimes the government would like us to believe that it is. All the predictions made by economic forecasters lead us to believe that any recovery will be slow and that we are not going to return to the kind of economic growth that we once knew. Put simply, we are facing an economy in which a large number of people are unemployed, bankruptcies have increased, inflation continues to soar and, in the last few days, we have seen the failure of the Canadian dollar. That is a clear indication of a failing economy.
National Training Act
It is not enough to recognize the over-all economic problems that we face, Mr. Speaker. There are other and more particular problems with employment and training. There are some very grave inequities in the way people are able to earn income. Some are able to make a pretty good living while others are not. I am thinking of groups normally designated as disadvantaged-women, natives, the handicapped and even immigrants.
I should like to say something about the employment of women. We all know that on average women earn something in the order of 60 per cent of the income that men earn. By and large they work in what are known as job ghettos. The technological changes of the future are a threat to the low paying jobs that women presently occupy. The microchip revolution will deskill a lot of jobs so that the work women presently do will require less skill and, as a result, they will lose earning power. There are other jobs that will become more highly skilled, of course, but it will be more difficult for women in the future to climb the ladder of their careers than it has in the past.
Most Canadians are aware that the vast majority of native people have neither the education nor the equality of opportunity that is necessary to be successful in the working world and to earn a decent income. They have been in this position for a long time, of course, but that is no justification for the situation continuing.
Handicapped people are also disadvantaged in the economy and in the job market. Very real barriers exist for handicapped people, not only in the physical sense of access to buildings where they might work and participate in community activities, but also in terms of attitude. We have not really learned to accept the handicapped person as someone with full rights of citizenship and the full right to earn a decent living.
Many immigrants were attracted to this country by the promise of prosperity, but recently some lured here to work in the garment industry, for example, have been disappointed. Rather than steady employment and a good income they have been faced with lay-offs, part-time employment and shattered dreams. Many of them work for less than the minimum wage and many are underemployed. I can think of a Philippino man who was trained and qualified as an engineer in his own country but found when he came to Canada that he could not use his skills and had to work as a draftsman. There are some people who feel that he may not have had the same standard of training as a Canadian engineer, but I would remind hon. members that the educational system in the Philippines was established by the United States and that the same training manuals are used there as are used in Canada. In fact, in Canada and in the Philippines, the education of engineers is modelled on the United States system, so there is no reason for the inequity that continues to exist.
The labour market not only demonstrates the inequitable and intolerable state of employment among disadvantaged groups but there is also a great deal of waste. There is waste of the great human potential that exists in this country. The

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
hopes, dreams and futures of our young people are being laid to waste. Our record high level of unemployment has reached almost two million in real terms and about half that number are young people. They are losing the opportunity to gain the training and experience which are necessary for them to work their way up in the job market. Not only are their hopes and dreams shattered by the present economic mess and lack of training, but there is another shocking problem that should not exist in any industrialized western democracy. The task force report entitled "Work for Tomorrow-Employment Opportunities for the '80s" identified the extent of functional illiteracy in this country. A very significant portion of our population does not have the basic education necessary to make a living in an industrialized society. There is a waste of human potential and a waste of economic potential as a result. If those people were given an opportunity to be functionally literate, they would be an asset to our society and to our economy.
All these problems-record high unemployment, inequities in the labour market, the waste of human potential-exist in a country that has very real and great potential, a country that has an educated population and great resources. A country like ours should not put up with these kinds of problems.
How has the government responded to the situation we face today? Its response has been disappointing, to say the least. It has been what I would describe as a public relations response. This bill, C-115, the legislative authority for the national training program, does not tell us a great deal about that program. It does not tell us what the government intends to do. In order to find out something about that, we have to go to the press releases issued by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). I am looking at one now dated May 21, 1982 in which he described the so-called new national training program. But it does not tell us a heck of a lot about what the program is going to look like either. It is a well-crafted document which certainly touches on all the key points. It mentions native people, handicapped people, women, and it mentions there will be new initiatives. But it does not tell us a heck of a lot about how they are going to do these things. It tells us they are going to train native people and others for national occupations, but no substance, no detail and no specifics. That is what I mean when I say it is a public relations response; it makes for good press releases and good speeches, but it has no substance.
I do not want you, Mr. Speaker, to accept my comments on the basis of my assertions alone. I would like to examine a few of the things mentioned in this national training program. The first thing I want to comment on is the approach to forecasting the kinds of jobs for which people will have to be trained. The proposed forecasting system is called the Canadian occupations projection system, or COPS for short. It is a macroeconomic system which involves consultation with various groups in society. It is a system devised by the same institution, the federal government, which has failed so dismally in the past in its predictions for job needs and training. But the real problem with the system is that it offers no real way of obtaining access to information about private sector investment intentions. Just
where do corporations intend to invest in the future and, therefore, what kinds of jobs will result and what kind of training do we have to put in place?
Of course, it is quite natural that a corporation would want to keep its investment decisions confidential because of competitive factors. You cannot just make this information available willy-nilly because your competitors will take advantage of it. Yet we must find a way if we are to be able in any way to forecast the kinds of jobs which will exist in the future.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, having a macroeconomic prediction model, or even consulting with other groups about what they want, is no substitute for an industrial strategy. An industrial strategy should involve public participation in the determination of investment decisions in this country over the coming years. In other words, where are we going to put our dollars, what kind of industry are we going to develop, and therefore what kind of labour market are we going to have? Without a well-thought-out industrial plan, without some public involvement in the direction of investment, we have really no way of knowing just what the economy is going to look like in the future.
I would like to move on to another aspect of this so-called national training program. I say so-called because it really is not all that it purports to be. There is a section in this bill dealing with industrial training, the essence of which is that it will provide incentive funds to industry to train workers on the job or in other settings. Well, Mr. Speaker, this is not new. A system based on incentives has been in place in this country now for quite some time. It is also a system which has led us to our present circumstances of extremely high unemployment and jobs which lack skilled workers. As a part of this system of training incentives there has been an effort to move funding away from community colleges which, of course, come under provincial jurisdiction. It looks like there will be a reduction of 10 per cent in funding to community colleges. I say that based on the fact that the guarantee being given to provincial governments and community colleges is that their funding will not fall below 90 per cent of what it was before. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that guarantee will become the ceiling. In effect, you will have community colleges, the basic instrument we have for training people, facing a reduction in funding. This comes at a time when there is no way they can afford to do with less.
Another aspect of this training policy, Mr. Speaker, is what is called national occupations. The federal government, by legislation, is going to take upon itself the authority to designate certain occupations as national occupations. It is going to say: okay, this is an occupation in which we need trained people and this is where we are going to put our money.
What is wrong with that, Mr. Speaker? The problem is that you have the same old department making the decision about where to put the money. They have dressed it up a bit by putting it in legislation and calling it a "national occupation", but if you still have the same employment department making decisions about where our dollars are going, our experience to date with regard to how successful that department has been in
June 4, 1982

terms of putting the money in the right place to produce the required trained workers leaves us with very little confidence that anything really constructive will come out of this legislative designation of national occupations.
This bill leaves the federal government in a neat little position of being able to respond to public pressure from time to time. For example, if we became aware suddenly of a great shortage of machinists, although it might be a little too late, if it became a public issue and a political issue, it would not be a hard task for the government to add that activity to the designated list of national occupations and tell the people that the government is doing something. The problem would be, of course, that it would be far too late.
This national training program claims that it will give women, natives and disabled people better access to training. That is on page 4 of the backgrounder, the federal proposals, the press release that I mentioned. That one line does not mean much. It is nice to know that the federal government intends to give natives, for example, better access to training. The government said the same thing in the last federal budget with regard to economic development. They had a line there that said there would be some $350 million for native economic development. Native leaders have called me and asked where that money is. They say they know it was in the budget, that they have been trying to find out from the government about it and they ask what they intend to do with it, how they intent to spend it, what shape the program will be that will be so financed. They cannot find out; they are worried that one day they will wake up and find the program has been laid down and they will have to live with it, regardless of the content or structure of the programs and without their really having any say about what the program should be. The same thing applies here. There is talk about giving natives better access to training. It would have been far better to get the native leadership involved in the development of that program before it was announced.
The government also claims that there will be better access to training for women. With the technological change going on in our society, with the microchip revolution, with the gaps in the career ladder that this is going to cause for women, it will be even more difficult than today for them to advance and reach a level of economic equality with men.
Women want not just a one-line mention in a press release. They want some real guarantees that they will have access to the highly skilled occupations that will be created by technological change. They want a real guarantee that they will get first crack at those jobs. They want to know that adequate and worth-while training will be provided so that they can move from low level occupations into the new highly skilled occupations, and therefore be able to jump the gap in the career ladder that is created by technological change.
Another aspect of this program is the skills growth fund. This is the fund of $108 million for facilities and equipment, to help in the updating of the training equipment available in institutions across the country. We do not know much about
National Training Act
that item from this press release. I wonder how far $108 million will go in this great big land.

speechtext: A drop in the bucket.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
We have ten provinces, and if you divide that sum equally it may mean only $10.8 million for each province.
It is not a great deal when you consider the expense of bringing facilities up to modern technological standards.
Over all, Mr. Speaker, this program touches all the right bases in terms of identifying the issues, but when you take a closer look at it and try to find out the specifics and what it means, it is like punching a pillow; you really cannot get at it. We do not have adequate information and we are not told what is really being intended. That is not an adequate response to the situation we are facing today of high unemployment, lack of skilled workers and inequities in the labour market. That is an inadequate response.
Some might believe that is the best that can be done. I think a lot more could be done, Mr. Speaker. We could find really concrete ways of working with the very difficult problems we face. We do not have to be superficial in our approach. We do not have to accept the manpower department programs as they have always been. We can have a positive impact upon the type of training that is to take place in this country. We could have a comprehensive training system that would meet the needs of our economy for the future and provide Canadians with real opportunities to train for interesting and exciting jobs in the future.
Let me give some examples, Mr. Speaker, to demonstrate what I have been saying, that it is possible to do better than what is proposed in this national training program. Going back to the question of the economy and jobs, what this country needs now, and needs badly, is an industrial strategy. It needs a plan to create manufacturing jobs throughout the country, not jobs in one region but jobs in all regions. It is obvious to everyone that the economic strategy this government has been following, based upon resource export, has really failed. That is literally demonstrated with the failure of the megaprojects in recent times. We need a plan for developing our industrial economy. We need a plan for investment in manufacturing, so that there will be jobs for which Canadians can be trained and to which people can look forward.
With regard to projecting what kind of positions people will need to be trained for, as my colleague from the Conservative Party mentioned, there was a joint submission from the Canadian Labour Congress and the Business Council on National Issues, a proposal for a labour market institute. This offers at least one real and concrete way of adding to the information that we have and will allow us to make better predictions about the jobs for which we need to train people. It offers an institutional setting in which researchers could talk to businessmen to find out something about their investment decisions without making the information generally available to the public. Therefore, this information about their investment decisions could be the basis for the kinds of prediction

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
the institution would make about training needs for the future. It would be a real way of bolstering, making more accurate, and placing a more solid data base under the projection system we use for making decisions concerning the jobs for which we are training people.
With regard to the system that we use to train people for predicted jobs, we need an industrial training system which is comprehensive, in the sense that it encourages and demands that all employers become involved in training. One of the main problems with training in the country today is that a very small percentage of employers train people for skilled jobs. Of course, those employers can be raided by other employers of those skilled workers once they have made an investment in them.
We must devise a system which makes it mandatory for all employers in the country to train and to contribute to the cost of training. This would be a way of ensuring that employers train and that there are skilled workers to fill the jobs of the future. Such a comprehensive industrial training system would view training as an investment. We would not have to rely only upon skilled immigrants, we would be training people who are in Canada to fill those skilled jobs.
Turning to the disadvantaged-and I will briefly mention native people-over the last few years there has been demonstrated success with what are called new careers programs. These programs may last several years in length of training. They take people with very low levels of education and train them for professional occupations, such as teachers, lawyers and doctors, over four or five years, and this results in a real difference in the income levels of these people. There is no mention of this in the national training program, but such a commitment would mean a real difference in the program. There is no mention of or commitment to a new career training strategy. If that is to be the intention, it should be spelled out.
With regard to women, we need a real assurance or some guarantee from the government that women who are displaced in the workplace as a result of technological change will have first crack at the jobs which come up, and that they will have adequate training in order to be ready and available for them.
In regard to the handicapped, a very good study was conducted by the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped entitled "Obstacles". A solid commitment should be spelled out to the very good recommendations in this report with regard to employment for the handicapped.
The problem of functional illiteracy was mentioned in another parliamentary report on manpower. It is a very severe problem in this country that saps the wealth of the nation. Why do we not have a war on functional illiteracy in this country? Is it not time that all Canadians should have an adequate education, at least an education which allows them to enter the labour market? There are many ways of approaching the difficult problems we face. I encourage the government to
look harder at the possibility of implementing some of these approaches to training and employment problems in the country.
In conclusion, unemployment in Canada is the highest it has been since the depression of the 1930s. When a real recovery begins-and there is no evidence of it yet occurring-it looks as though it will be very slow. The market is begging for skilled workers, yet we continue to spend billions of dollars on training in a haphazard manner. Canadians could be doing the work which we all know needs to be done. Canadian factories could be producing a cornucopia of wealth. Women, natives, handicapped persons, immigrants, youths and all Canadians could be trained for skilled jobs. To paraphrase a former practitioner of our trade, politics, the art of the possible, some people see things as they are and ask why; I dream not the impossible dream but of real things yet to be, and ask why not?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising in the House today to express my support for Bill C-115, an Act to establish a national program for occupational training, because I am convinced that this legislation will make a major contribution toward adjusting our training system in Canada to the demands of the electronic age. I must admit that I would have preferred to take part in a debate in more cheerful circumstances. I would have preferred to praise our accomplishments across Canada, our abundant wealth and our very advantageous economic situation. Unfortunately, the situation is quite different, not to say alarming. Mr. Speaker, I have decided to take part in this debate for two reasons. First of all, because the unemployment rate in Canada, although it is impossible to give the exact figures, has reached a record high, and although we can say that all industrialized countries are faced with this kind of problem, I do not think we can draw any consolation from a comparison with other countries, although on the other hand, such a comparison does oblige us to be more realistic and to recognize that Canada, notwithstanding its constant and renewed efforts, will never be able to insulate itself from other countries and their problems, just as they do not insulate themselves from the prosperity enjoyed by industrialized countries.
My second reason, Mr. Speaker, is that I have had the honour and the privilege of sitting on a seven-member task force, one member of which, I am sad to say, is no longer with us, and here, I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to our colleague Bruce Lonsdale, who passed away several months ago, and who made a major contribution to the work of our committee. The task force, Mr. Speaker, was fortunate in being able to travel across Canada and to find out for itself, during often very spirited discussions with the public, about the real problems of unemployment and solutions that could be considered. The committee, on which I acted as cochairman with the member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), submitted 186 recommendations. The Minister of Employment
June 4, 1982

and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has accepted several of these recommendations, and I would like to take this opportunity to thank him and to ask him to continue implementing of the basic recommendations of this report on employment opportunities for the '80s.
Mr. Speaker, although there are continuing regional and sectorial manpower shortages, Canadians are experiencing the highest unemployment levels in 40 years. Although this unusual situation is very cold comfort for those who are unemployed, it does point to a number of shortcomings in Canada's manpower policy and leads us to expect that our problems will soon get worse. Until now, Canada has been unable to meet the demand for skilled workers in the traditional trades and it has been unable to adjust to the needs of a developing economy. Until the middle of the seventies, most of our requirements for skilled manpower were filled by immigrant workers from abroad. However, a rise in the standard of living in the European emigration countries led to a serious drop in the number of immigrants. The resulting decline in the numbers of skilled manpower has given us an economy that is plagued by inflation while at the same time not being able to provide enough jobs for less skilled workers. This situation has been aggravated by a recession that is both national and international. Unskilled workers are the last to be hired and the first to be fired.
Businesses can no longer operate at full capacity are being restructured and that, as a result, less skilled workers and those with the least seniority are being laid off first. This has led to a decline in the number of on-the-job training programs and thus in the number of opportunities for workers to gain experience. Consequently, today's recession is contributing to tomorrow's shortage of skilled workers. In extreme cases, recessionary pressures are weakening the economy's structures to the point where businesses that could be productive are going bankrupt. Our manpower policy must cope with these problems, first of all, by restructuring Canadian industry so as to facilitate adjustment of the labour market to new demands. Subsequently, workers already on the labour market must be trained or retrained for the trades that are necessary to a proper functioning of the economy. Finally, jobs must be structured to take account of the specific needs of workers. For instance, allowances must be made for the particular needs of the increasing number of women who are carrying a twofold responsibility for work in the home and in the labour force.
In addition to the recurring weaknesses of our manpower policy in these areas, Canada's decision-makers will be confronted with further major problems during this decade. The ongoing trend toward opening up occupations and the wave of investment for the purpose of integrating new technology should lead us to expect important changes in the sectorial and occupational balance of regions where there is a manpower demand. If Canada is unable to respond to the new demand for
National Training Act
skilled manpower, it may be prevented from upgrading its production potential and jobs will literally have to be exported. The arrival of fewer young workers on the labour market means on the one hand that the economy will not have to absorb a large number of workers with more experience as was the case during the last decade. On the other hand, as the average age of the workers increases, adjustment to the new requirements will have to depend to a greater extent on the retraining of those who are already part of the labour force. Finally, the women's rate of participation is expected to go on increasing while the service sector, which has been the traditional source of female employment, will probably be the most affected by the technological changes, and especially by the microelectronics revolution.
The two basic questions concerning training are how and where it is given and who pays for it. How do we achieve a balance between experience and on-the-job training on the one hand and academic training on the other ? A changing economy needs a labour force that not only is specialized, but that also has transferable specializations. Obviously it is easier to learn some of the trades on the job and a different approach is needed for others. The lack of basic training is restricting many Canadians to unskilled jobs and is virtually excluding them from training and retraining programs. Over four million Canadians are functionally illiterate. On-the-job experience cannot teach them to read or write any better or to improve their marginal situation in relation to the labour force as a whole. On the other hand, to the extent that training is transferable, each employer is tempted to attract specialized workers away from other employers since he can then benefit from these workers without any cost to him. It is because of this market deficiency that the government has had to subsidize training facilities through its tax revenues. However, these programs which range from university and college courses to manpower training programs have too often ignored the requirements of the labour market.
On a national level, there is a shortage of engineers and a surplus of arts graduates. Regional manpower programs have trained workers for jobs that require little specialization in areas affected by chronic unemployment. Financing must be more selective and the programs better co-ordinated. In addition, people often say that a given training program does not meet the specific needs of the industry. Attempts to reduce work situations reproduced in laboratories and workshops have proven costly and outdated and they have shown that our teaching institutions do not have the required resources at their disposal. Universities have had to deal with both basic training and fundamental research. We shall need a much broader spectrum of on-the-job training programs to match theory with practice.
While off-the-job training has sometimes been inadequate, the very serious shortage of specialized workers in the fields that traditionally require an apprenticeship period point to the

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
obvious failure of this procedure in Canada as compared with students trained in teaching institutions. Apprentices are often laid off during a recession. Besides, apprenticeship programs are often spread out over conventional four-year periods without any consideration for the actual requirements of the trade. The government has already implemented various industrial training subsidization programs, but we obviously have to do more. Already the fundamental question of who should pay for this training and who should distribute the funds is being asked.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, when I was travelling across Canada and consulting with the people, the most frequent comments we heard were the following: young people realize they are trained in skills where there is absolutely no prospect of short, medium, or long-term employment. They complained all across Canada that they were insufficiently and inadequately counselled; in that regard, this legislation fulfils that requirement in part. Another comment we heard was that often young people do receive theoretical education but no adequate practical training, which prevents them from filling jobs within a reasonable time-frame. Those two basic complaints were heard over and over and over again, Mr. Speaker. There are, in my opinion, five training principles that should be adhered to and closely examined. First, more specialized training should be provided in Canada. Second, more on-the-job training should be provided. Third, a greater number of Canadians should be attracted to highly skilled trades. This is one of the major objectives of the legislation now before us. Four, ongoing education, retraining and upgrading should be provided in order to meet the increasing demand for new technology and the changing concept of competition on the world markets. Five, fair and equitable funding should be studied in depth.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on those training aspects, and say a few words on in-plant training. During our travels, we often heard that in the area of training it was essential to give higher priority to on-the-job training in order to meet industry's current needs. The Canadian government will spend $166 million in 1982-83 to help employers provide training that is often costly and time-consuming. Employers who wish to train workers or upgrade training in trades such as tool-making, welding, industrial maintenance mechanics, electronics and engineering technicians, oil production and other first-class trades will be given priority in the allotment of federal funds. The current critical trade skills training program will be integrated within the industrial training program, and CTST training will be improved. Such initiatives are aimed at helping the industry set up the structures needed to train each year 10,000 highly skilled workers by 1984-85.
In addition to training workers in the critical trades, the industrial training program will stress training in the trades
where job demand is high, the retraining of workers affected by technological and industrial changes, the training of the unemployed, the training of women in fields where jobs are usually held by men, and the training of adults with specific needs. This scheme strikes me as very interesting and encouraging, Mr. Speaker, and I urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to pursue his efforts in that direction.
With regard to institutional training, Mr. Speaker, I should also like to make a few comments. As we pointed out in our report on employment opportunities, institutional training should complement in-plant training by giving higher priority to the critical trades, that is those where a shortage of skilled labour exists. I believe the minister got the message. The number of skilled workers can be increased not only by extending the traditional apprenticeship training but also by giving some training prior to the apprenticeship stage provided by provincial educational institutions. That is why the federal government is willing to finance a major expansion of preapprenticeship training in the critical trades, provided the provincial governments agree to include that training in their apprenticeship programs, and provided there is a real demand in the industry for that type of trainees. The federal government will also buy more pre-job training courses, because requirements having been increased in such trades as computer programming, industrial design and word processing. Thus, training prior to apprenticeship and employment will be available, which it is not at the present time, enabling one to acquire skills to a higher or a lesser degree. Simultaneously, the federal government will progressively abandon its purchases of non-productive courses or reduce them according to the actual needs of the economy. The funds the government intends to inject into training will also go to the training in school of apprentices in the Red Seal jobs and other trades where demand in high.
Mr. Speaker, I said that a fifth important aspect of training that bears scrutiny is that of financing. I should like to repeat Recommendation 40 of our task force report on employment opportunities which suggested the following solution to the government, and I quote:
40. To help finance industrial training, the government should establish a refundable tax on salaries, wages and other remuneration (a payroll tax-credit system), in the following manner:
(a)	A payroll tax should be applied to employers, equal to a designated percentage (perhaps 0.5%) of their payroll.
(b)	Any amount of money up to the designated percentage of payroll spent on training approved by existing training authorities, or training leading to a degree from a recognized education or training institution, should be credited against the payroll tax.
Mr. Speaker, that is a suggestion we have made, which the minister has not yet implemented but to which he has certainly given consideration, for it is a significant part of what I feel is the answer to the problem of training funding.
June 4, 1982

We need the National Training Act that is now before us to upgrade our training system, in order to better respond to the challenge of technological change. To be able to fill the positions of tomorrow, Canadians must have the opportunity to take updated training courses using modern equipment, and that is specifically the purpose of the National Training Act. This bill will authorize the setting up of the skills growth fund, the easing of requirements that have limited in the past our capacity to train specialized workers, as well as the introduction of incentives to retrain workers. All these elements are prior conditions to the upgrading of our training system. This upgrading is urgently needed because technological developments are rapidly changing our daily lives.
For instance, our letters are typed on word processors. Surgeons use laser beams for microsurgery and our children do not simply attend ordinary day camps any more, but computer camps. Moreover, most job opportunities available nowadays are for men and women familiar with digital components, micro-processors, optical fibers and computers. Our capacity to adapt to these changes will have a strong impact on Canada's economic growth, productivity and trade balance. On a more personal level, we are offering every Canadian the possibility of stimulating and rewarding professions.
Pessimists fear that the technological revolution will open the door to massive unemployment. In West Germany, for instance, some foresee that office work will soon be 40 per cent automated, which will cause millions of office workers to lose their jobs. According to a Canada Council report, if we delay promoting the development of technologies in the areas of micro-processors and telecommunications, we will lag behind more advanced nations for quite a long time. A great many operations in the manufacturing industry would become obsolete overnight. Our trade balance, already precarious, might never recover. Structural unemployment could result in permanent unemployment for many Canadians, a lowering of our standard of living and possibly compel some to emigrate. That is what the Canada Council is saying will happen unless we make all-encompassing changes. Although the Canada Council has elected to paint such a grim picture of the negative consequences the technological revolution may entail, Canadians are nevertheless aware of the urgent need to make changes now. We must promote technological innovations by providing funds for research and development and devising the most modern and efficient training system. As an optimist, I feel that the technological revolution is offering us a unique opportunity to make the best possible use of our most precious assets, which are our human resources, increase productivity and create new jobs. In the area of computer graphics for instance, computer assisted design and manufacturing might make incredible increases in productivity possible, if we put the available technology to work. This new technology will liberate workers from tedious and repetitive jobs. They will be able to control the quality of their own work. Moreover, the kinds of jobs created through the practical application of
National Training Act
advanced technology, if we approach them the right way, may be rid of the obstacles and prejudices that are at the present time hindering professional groups.
By shifting the emphasis toward trades in great demand, the new training legislation will make it possible to increase retraining opportunities. Women who hold most clerical jobs in offices and in the service sector will be disproportionately affected by the advent of new technology and we must see to it that they are given the opportunity to upgrade their skills or, if they prefer, switch to fields which so far have been the preserve of men. These past few years, Canadians have gained international recognition in the field of technological innovation. For instance, the Telidon system developed by Canada's Department of Communications is now being widely acknowledged as the world's leading videotex/teletex technology. In addition, our reputation has been greatly enhanced in international quarters with the unveiling of the space shuttle remote-controlled manipulator arm made in Canada. The National Training Act will help us benefit from such achievements. It will enable us to ensure that we have modern and efficient training facilities to train the number of workers needed by industry. It will also make it easier to alleviate some of our strict and restrictive requirements and to offer better incentives for retraining workers left behind by the industrial revolution.
The legislation introduced by the minister will pave the way toward faster economic growth and a better employment outlook for Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I feel that this bill should be adopted soon, before the end of the session. This legislation will give us the legislative authority to go ahead with major initiatives such as the skills growth fund. This fund is of vital importance if we seriously aim at training enough highly skilled workers to meet the needs of our economy, but the money will not be available unless the National Training Act does become law. Without that authority, we cannot earmark funds to build or expand a single training institution, no matter how urgently it may be needed. As it is, the institutions we do have fall far short of training all the skilled labour at the rate required by the industry. Unless we greatly speed up the rate of expansion, we can expect severe shortages of about 9,000 skilled workers a year over the next five years. Capital expenditures of that magnitude call for huge investments. The provinces are busy setting up programs that will require investments of many million dollars. For its part, the federal cabinet has set aside a 3108-million fund for that purpose for the current and next fiscal years, but those funds are frozen until the bill is passed.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer briefly to the basic aspects of this legislative measure, first and foremost the skills growth fund. Manpower sources and the existing training institutions will not turn out enough expert technicians and tradesmen to meet the demand in the eighties. With a view to

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
promoting manpower training in high priority jobs, the federal government will establish under the new act the skills growth fund, in co-operation with the provinces, so as to expand or upgrade our technical training equipment and facilities. The provinces, the industries or non-profit organizations could be asked to administer the institutions. They would also be responsible for training designated groups such as native people in skills in great demand.
Second, the legislation will broaden the range of training courses provided as well as the classes of workers eligible to take those courses. It will provide a list of priority skills and the variety of courses available in those fields. Under the new legislation, higher allowances may be paid to laid-off workers in designated industries and areas, under the special industry and labour adjustment program, who decide to retrain in order to acquire skills in great demand when a high rate of vacancy is not expected in their former occupation. The allowances paid would increase insurable earnings or unemployment insurance benefits from 60 to 70 per cent or if the benefits have expired, additional benefits would be paid if the workers are enrolled in retraining programs.
Third, the bill will provide higher financial allowances in order to encourage laid-off apprentices to acquire skills in trades where there is a shortage of manpower and workers to retrain in fields where technological change has caused their lay-offs but where jobs are still available. Additional special allowances would be paid to laid-off apprentices attending critical trade skills training courses. The additional payments would be added to other forms of income support.
Fourth, the bill will remove the present requirement that adults have completed their studies 12 months before enrolling for training courses to enable young drop-outs to attend those courses that are essential to them. As for skilled workers, the new legislation will authorize the Employment Commission to remove the present requirement under which a trainee must wait a year before enrolling in a training institution. In some cases, when young people or members of special groups have left the regular school system and wish to acquire new skills, a delay of one year is a real waste of human resources at a time when the need is greatest.
Fifth, under the new legislation, workers will be allowed to receive a more specialized training for a period longer than today's 52-week limit. This provision, which will remove the 52-week limit for training courses and allow the financing of training programs over a longer period, is of major importance and it is essential that it be approved as soon as possible.
Highly-specialized training programs in occupations of national importance would benefit the most from this provision. Removal of this restriction will also make it possible to combine preparatory courses with personal training on the basis of existing opportunities. This would benefit many
workers, such as women who re-enter the labour market and native people who need such a combination to acquire skills and find jobs. Sixth, the new legislation will provide support for employers who have to train highly-specialized Canadian workers abroad. Under this bill, the Commission would be able to negotiate with the employers training agreements for programs-

Mr. Speaker, you know of my special interest in this subject, so you will understand that I am delighted to be able to participate in this debate on this day. Unfortunately, this is not a very good day to discuss a measure like this, in light of the statistics announced earlier showing that we have record unemployment.
June 4, 1982

Not even in the deepest of the depression did we have the numbers of unemployed we have today.
Mir. Deans: We are leading the industrialized world.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
What the statistics do not readily reveal is that over half of the 1.25 million unemployed-and that is only the official statistic; the number is closer to two million-are under the age of 24, and that is a serious indictment respecting the ability of this government to come to grips with a very serious situation.
It is very difficult to discuss this bill without providing the backdrop of what it is intended to do and the problem it is supposed to solve. Many of my colleagues have repeatedly said that we have entered a new era of technological and industrial revolution, one that will proceed and accelerate at a pace ten times as fast as the industrial revolution which has been under way for 200 years. If that is so and if all the promises and opportunities this new technological and microelectronic revolution will bring with it are realized, I am very much afraid this bill will do very little to respond to these opportunities and challenges. However, to be fair, it is a small step and it is in a general direction, so we are looking forward to discussing this matter in committee further and providing the minister with some ideas that we on this side of the House have developed.
I am rather pleased that in his speeches the minister uses some statistics that I have assembled and some from reports made by his department and others who have studied what I call the human resource paradox. There are major industrial projects, particularly in new industries, that cannot proceed because of a serious shortage of manpower skills on the one hand and, on the other, because there are large numbers of unemployed who have no opportunity to find work.
The minister and the government must come to grips with the fact that in the post-war period it was commonplace, every time manpower skills were needed, to bring in well trained, seasoned immigrants to fill the jobs. The average Canadian workers were left to find jobs as labourers and acquire skills as they went along. That would not help us respond to the challenges and the opportunities of the last ten or 15 years of this century and the beginning of the next.
This bill is supposed to carve out a role for the federal government to re-enter or to broaden its participation in the field of education. We all know that since confederation there has been an ongoing dispute between the federal and provincial governments. The provinces have guarded their jurisdiction over culture and education very jealously, rejecting every effort of the federal government to carve out a role for itself. My illustrious colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) outlined for us how the federal government from time to time, and with varying degrees of success, has intervened in this area.
There is a new twist, however, in the way that the minister proposes to intervene in the field of education. May I say at the outset that I agree with the notion that the federal government will have a major role in this area. It will have to pay for
National Training Act
what I call its deliberate policy of neglect of our educational system which is supposed to train young people for the transition from school to work.
At the end of this month another 200,000 young people will graduate from our schools and will enter the job market for the first time. The provinces seem to think that their role is complete then, and that unless a young person goes on to university it is the responsibility of the federal government to find him a job and, if that is not possible, to find a way of getting him on the unemployment insurance rolls.
The federal government should begin to establish a national focus for education. The minister has proposed a new definition of the word occupation. Clause 2 of the bill reads in part as follows:
"occupational training" means any instruction, other than university instruction, that provides a person with skills for, or improves a person's skills in, an occupation;
So occupational training is no longer regarded as education and, as a result, the federal government feels justified in entering the field. I am not worried about that because I think we should seize any opportunity to help in this area. To be educated in school will now mean that the schools look after academic requirements. The minister will probably agree with me that the primary and secondary school system is geared to fulfilling academic requirements-everyone wants their children to become doctors, lawyers and engineers and nobody wants their children to scramble through life in a blue collar job.
I think that governments, unions, schools and industry all have a role to play in removing the stigma attached to blue collar trades. Some of these do quite well, I am told. It is reported that some plumbers make more money than doctors these days, so a stigma should not be attached to a blue collar job. Nevertheless, our education system is still geared to the academic side which prepares young people for university.
I have assembled some statistics on how many young people who graduate go on to university. I became interested in the subject after reading a report of a commission appointed by our OECD trading partners. It has studied the educational system in this country and made some recommendations. These were rather startling. It found that Canada has spent more money than any other country in the western world-and one can assume that means any country in the world-on educational facilities. In the sixties there was a great push to build new schools, learning institutions and universities. Money was no object, and we outclassed every other country in our generosity to our educational system.
The commission found that the product of these schools was mediocre in comparison to the educational skills, academic or vocational, of other systems. That finding offended me and 1 became interested in the subject. Having studied it, I then decided to write my own paper and to that end I assembled some statistics.
I found that about 30 per cent of people who passed grade nine and entered the last three years of secondary schooling

June 4, 1982
National Training Act
did not complete school. In general they enter the labour market and find jobs washing dishes, driving trucks, or labouring in the hopes that they will acquire skills as they go along. Too often they just stand around on the streets, particularly when the economy is in the state it is in now. Their hopes and dreams are shattered and no one knows what happens to them.
Of the 70 per cent that complete school, only 30 per cent advance to post-secondary institutions, and of those, only 19 per cent get a degree. So 70 per cent of the graduating school population on the job market is totally unskilled and 200,000 of them will enter the job market at the end of this month.
The OECD people, and I in my report, looked at a number of other countries and what they are doing to overcome this problem. It is no secret, Mr. Speaker, that I grew up and went to school in another country. Therefore I have personal experience in this particular area, so it was not very difficult for me to make comparisons. The secondary school system in most of the industrial countries we compete with is a dual system. Young people make their decision on what they will do for the rest of their lives at a much earlier age, usually 14 or 15, in consultation with their parents and guidance counsellors. When you consider, Mr. Speaker, that it costs the taxpayer $3,200 a year to keep a student in school, and when you consider that 70 per cent of those in grades 11 and 12 are totally bored by the system and will not get anything out of it, that is getting to be pretty ridiculous.
When I moved my family here my son and daughter were to go to grade 13. I asked an official of the Ontario Department of Education why, for heaven's sakes, in this province there are 13 grades of school instead of 12, as is the case in most other provinces? The reason stated was that we cannot afford to send out another 100,000 people to stand around on street corners. In fact, the official said, it is a glorified babysitting service.
It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that I see some failings in this bill, particularly where the minister says he will use some of this new-found money to build additional educational facilities and buy additional equipment. I know the minister has read my report, and he complimented me on it. It is not, of course, the be all and end all. Some people say the attitudes in our country are not conducive to the kind of dual system that exists in Germany and Japan and in other countries with which we compete. However, I ask myself from time to time whether this is not the time for government and politicians to change their attitude toward education because we know the system is failing and our young people are not properly served. Someone has to do something. Now, who should do so if not our senior levels of government?
There are other components of this bill which worry me, for example, where it says that those people who can prove they have not been in school for at least a 12-month period can qualify for vocational or occupational training courses. There is a qualification, and I respect that, that the commission or
inspector can waive that particular provision. But why is it in there in the first place? According to the report of the OECD inspectors, we are not doing too bad a job in adult training. Our regional colleges are doing a good job in training our adults, but we are spending most of our time and resources in chasing the horse after it has left the barn. Neither this bill nor any other measure laid before us since I have been here has been designed in any way to come to grips with the root cause of the problem: to challenge our young people at a much earlier age to make a decision.

I challenge the hon. member to tell me why it is that at the present time over half of the unemployed are under the age of 24. The fact is that our educational system has failed them miserably, and our senior governments have pursued a policy of deliberate neglect in terms of looking after the legitimate needs and aspirations of our young people.
There are other sections in this bill that we will certainly want to examine when we get it into committee, but I would like to think that members have an open mind. Certainly this bill is not conducive to making amendments which would lead us to these kinds of far-reaching proposals which have been made. The minister, from time to time, like his colleagues, indulges in making accusations to the effect that the opposition only criticizes and never has any constructive ideas to put forward. I want to serve notice on him that we will bring to committee some constructive ideas, and we would be very pleased if the minister would come to the committee with the same kind of open mind. He is talking about spending a lot of money, and we want to be assured that it will be spent in the right direction.
Another portion of the bill which is nothing new is the clause which says that no occupational course can last longer than 52 weeks. I recognize the fact that the commission can waive that provision, but I question its being in the bill in the first place. The problem is that as we look for national occupations, I assume the minister does not intend these to be occupations which are needed from time to time. I would think the government intends to identify certain national occupations toward which young persons or adults would work to achieve a certificate, and these occupations would be identified as such. It would not necessarily be the job of a welder; rather, I would say, that of a forestry technician, a baker or a chef. It does not matter what kind of learning institution you are in, it takes longer than 52 weeks to become a millwright. In fact, I maintain there is no institution in this country, nor would you be
June 4, 1982

able to create one, that would be able to respond to the challenge of the new technological revolution. In future, training will have to be carried on in the actual workplace.
The dual system I envisage would accommodate that. Industry would play a much greater role in training young people. In many other industrialized countries industry is compelled to assume that role. They are penalized through the tax system if they do not, and are rewarded in the same way if they oversubscribe to the programs. The schools and colleges then play a role in backing up the training which goes on in industry.
If you look at national occupations or vocations, Mr. Speaker, then you have to design programs which will last a lot longer than 52 weeks. In fact, for most of the occupations I mentioned, be they that of a millwright or a computer technician, and I could rattle off 40 or 50 others, the courses should probably run for three to four years. You cannot learn to be an electrician in 52 weeks and be able to market your skill in competition with people who have worked in the trade for a long time. The training would not necessarily require the construction of new buildings or the provision of new equipment. We have a lot of fine facilities, particularly in the secondary schools, which are underutilized.
For the information of my friend to the left, who seems to be over-reacting to some of the things I said, let me say that I get a lot of mail from teachers. I sent 5,000 copies of my report particularly to schools and school boards. I get a lot of response from teachers who tell me it is about time that somebody talked about these things openly, because teachers are incredibly frustrated.

speechtext:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons be appointed to evolve and bring before the Parliament of Canada a bill to provide for the structural reform of the Senate of Canada;
That nine Members of the House of Commons, to be designated at a later date, be Members on the part of this House on the Special Joint Committee;
That the Committee have the power to appoint from among its Members such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable and necessary and to delegate to such subcommittees all or any of their powers except the power to report directly to the House;
That the Committee have the power to sit during sittings and adjournments of the House of Commons;
That the Committee have the power to report from time to time, to send for persons, papers and records, and to examine witnesses and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the Committee;
That the Committee have the power to adjourn from place to place within Canada and to hold public hearings and consult fully with all provincial governments and Members of the legislative assemblies of the provinces as well as with the federal government and all Members of Parliament and Senators;

June 4, 1982
Senate Reform
That the Committee be empowered to retain the services of advisers to assist in its work; and that it also be empowered to retain the professional, clerical and stenographic help as may be required;
That the Committee submit its report not later than November 1, 1982;
That the quorum of the Committee be six Members, whenever a vote, resolution or other decision is taken, so long as both Houses are represented and that the Joint Chairmen be authorized to hold meetings, to receive evidence and authorize the printing thereof, when six Members are present so long as both Houses are represented;
That a Message be sent to the Senate requesting that that House do unite with this House for the above purpose and to select, if the Senate deems it to be advisable, Members to act on the proposed Special Joint Committee; and
That the Committee consider the following documents before submitting its report and bringing forward a bill to provide for the structural reform of the
Senate:
