He said: Mr. Speaker, I almost feel like starting by indicating that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) that this House pass this motion at the earliest opportunity so that in fact we can proceed with the motion as it is on the Order Paper.
I want to indicate that I have not moved any motion to that effect. 1 simply said that I feel like moving a motion to that effect and that it might be passed today so that the House could move forward with this motion.
This motion requests that a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to evolve and bring before the Parliament of Canada a bill to provide for the structural reform of the Senate of Canada. I am not going to read the motion, because it is fairly extensive, on the understanding that it will be included in its entirety in Hansard.
I want to underscore several parts of this motion and read them in to Hansard a second time, that is, that the committee consider the following documents before submitting its report and bringing forth a bill to provide for the structural reform of the Senate:
First, Bill C-640, an act to provide for structural reform of the Senate of Canada,
Second, the report of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution, 1972,
Third, Bill C-60, the Constitutional Amendment Bill, 1978,
Fourth, the Report of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution, 1978,
Fifth, the Report of the Special Senate Committee on the Constitution, 1978,
Sixth, British Columbia's Constitutional Proposals, 1978,
Seventh, the Report of the Task Force on Canadian Unity, 1979,
Eighth, the Report of the Constitutional Committee of the Quebec Liberal Party, 1980,
Ninth, the Report on Certain Aspects of the Canadian Constitution, 1980.
All these reports or papers, if you wish, deal with the reform of the Senate.
There are two aspects I wish to debate today. One is the need for Senate reform and some of the concepts incorporated in Bill C-640. The other is the process itself for structural Senate reform.
Mr. Speaker, I want to touch on the second part first, the process for structural Senate reform.
I have been in this House now for three years and I remember, as a provincial member and a member of a provincial cabinet, that for some 12 years the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) with the Premiers across the land, held first ministers' conferences to patriate the Constitution and reform the Constitution. They simply got nowhere. They held meeting after meeting after meeting and came to no conclusion and had no success.
It was not until the process was initiated by this House that the process of patriation and the incorporation of a Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and the evolution of an amending formula, finally reached success.
It was this House that took action by unanimous consent on May 9, 1980. It was this House that set up a joint committee of this House and the Senate to look at all aspects of a charter of rights and freedoms.
When this House took action directly, then things began to happen. So I am saying, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the process for Senate reform, that we must move to a similar type of action as we did with constitutional patriation and constitutional reform.
When this House and this Parliament puts together a proposal that is sound in every aspect, and then the Prime Minister goes to the Premiers with it, generally there is some form of agreement. But as long as the process was one of ten Premiers and the Prime Minister, or the 11 first ministers, getting together for a talk session, nothing ever happened. For 12 years that process went on.
I say again that until this House took very specific action, nothing really happened. But once this House took specific action then indeed we succeeded in repatriating the Constitution, with the entrenched Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and even in the evolution and acceptance of an amending formula.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am proposing through this Motion No. 66 that a similar type of process be undertaken, that we agree to the establishment of a joint committee of this House and the other place and that this committee be allowed to travel from one end of the nation to the other, and indeed consult with the
June 4, 1982

premiers, consult the provincial governments, and review all the past literature, and hold public hearings, if necessary, in regard to the meaning of the Senate itself. Then it can bring before this House a specific bill for Senate structural reform and also present the bill at the same time to the other place.
I am convinced that if we pursue, as the Parliament of Canada, this type of process, we will be successful in regard to Senate reform.
The next question is: why is Senate reform necessary? Henri Bourassa once said that Senate reform "comes periodically like other forms of epidemics and current fevers". He was right. Our history, especially our recent history, is littered with the forgotten remnants of proposals, studies and legislative initiatives which tried to breathe new life into an institution that has been wasting away for over 100 years. The fact is that reform of the Senate will not wait much longer. We have reached a point in our national development where we must make our institutions more responsive to every facet of Canadian society. There is a crisis of confidence in these institutions which has exacerbated regional and provincial alienation.
Over the last 20 years, economic, cultural and sociological developments have radically altered the face of Canada. Institutional reform is imperative, not only to respond to these developments, but to allow us to confront future challenges and problems, confident that our institutions can cope with the complexity of the problems before them.
Although the patriation of the Constitution with a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and an amending formula will help to revitalize our institutions, the debate surrounding patriation has unfortunately accentuated the acrimony and alienation felt in some parts of the country, particularly out west, because there is no clause for ownership of property. We must now take the reform process one step further to lessen ill feelings and tensions which have arisen. The west needs Senate reform; it needs a voice at the centre which represents the regions. This was the identified need for the Senate in the first place in Macdonald's time. Senate structural reform is necessary so that the provinces and regions can be represented directly at the centre in a meaningful way.
I have worked on Senate reform for quite a number of years. I have written a number of letters and have made a number of proposals in past years, but perhaps the two most appropriate initiatives which I took were to structure and introduce Bill C-640 and to place Motion No. 66 on the Order Paper, so that somehow or other this parliamentary institution could move in a meaningful way toward Senate reform.
I believe a special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate to investigate Senate reform and to report back to Parliament is a necessity. Such a committee would consult fully with all provincial governments and members of legislative assemblies, as well as with the federal government and all members of this institution. As I said earlier, this is an approach which can work and is more likely
Senate Reform
to succeed than allowing first ministers to do something which in the past they have always failed to achieve.
Bill C-640, an act to provide for the structural reform of the Senate of Canada, was intended to highlight the need for Senate reform as the first constitutional priority following the patriation of the Constitution. It sought to provide representation and balance in Parliament of the national, regional and provincial interests. I have proposed that the Senate be composed, to represent the national interest, of 150 senatorial chairs, and that these senatorial chairs be representative of five natural regions in Canada, with each region providing 30 senators to the Parliament of Canada. Also I proposed that the provincial interests be represented in the Senate by five senators for each province, appointed by the provinces and responsible to the provincial legislative assemblies. Furthermore, the bill was structured to provide the Senate body and each individual member with stability, continuity, accountability, legitimacy and independence.
I want to touch briefly upon each of these points in my remaining time. In regard to stability, each existing Senate member is permitted to complete his or her appointment in accordance with the terms of appointment. Each new senator is appointed for a minimum of six years, and then will have to return to the people to seek reconfirmation. It would be a form of election, a half-way situation between an appointed Senate and an elected Senate. Also I should say that it would be inappropriate to attempt to change the existing tenure of any senator who was elected or selected upon an existing system.
In regard to continuity, the transition from the old senatorial regime to the new one is structured so that only approximately one third of the senators would be up for reconfirmation every third year. Although I have had many second thoughts on this particular point, I now believe strongly that reconfirmation should occur only every six years. This presents an interesting complexity of senators within a restructured Senate in the future, if reconfirmation is held only on a six-year basis.
Let us imagine the situation where, from one end of this nation to the other, every six years senators initially appointed had to return to the people to seek reconfirmation in each province. Let us imagine a number of regional senators having to go back to the regions to seek reconfirmation. I think it would have a dramatic effect upon all Canada. I think senators would become important, and they would have to account for their usefulness in this institution to the people of the provinces and to the regions they represent. They would be accountable directly to the people they represent in this institution.
In regard to legitimacy, senators now lack legitimacy because they are appointed by one person, namely, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), they serve to the age of 75 years and are accountable individually and collectively to no one but themselves and perhaps to the person who appointed them. Lawmakers or lawgivers must surely gain legitimacy for their powers directly, or at least indirectly, from the people. Therefore, in the bill I have proposed they are appointed by all the people's representatives, either provincially or federally, and

June 4, 1982
Senate Reform
must go directly back to the people for reconfirmation rather than be appointed by one man only.
In regard to independence, under the new bill a senator can and will be able to maintain non-partisanship if he or she so wishes.
This is only one bill. This is only one alternative for Senate structural reform. As I indicated at the beginning of my speech, there are many alternatives. The structural reform of the Senate has been investigated and there are enough reports on that proposal to fill a suitcase.
The question which has been before most of us is whether it should be an appointed or an elected Senate. Surely the only acceptable process is one that is half-way in between. An elected Senate would permit directions which would not be acceptable to our system of government in Canada. I hope that hon. members and the government would seriously consider beginning a new process of senatorial reform similar to what it did in connection with constitutional patriation and constitutional reform. If it does, I believe that the other place can experience reform at the earliest opportunity and become a very effective representation of the regions and provinces in this place.
I suggest to you that much of the ferment which exists out west, such as western separatism, which I discount and reject, has been a result of inadequate direct representation by the provinces and regions in the Parliament of Canada. Senate structural reform must be one of the top priorities of additional constitutional reform from now on.

Whether that is the kind of proposition we would want to consider in the House-to have separate Indian representation-is certainly not something to which I want to commit myself now. However, it is an interesting subject which should be thoroughly examined and debated. New Zealand does have that kind of system with regard to the Maori population. I believe there are people with opinions from both sides of the fence as to how that system works now, but I suspect that the Maori population is still favourable to that idea even though their representation, which I believe
numbers only four, is not very significant considering the number of Maoris as a percentage of the total population of New Zealand.
Although I should not create new issues, issues which have not been raised in this motion, I did take issue with another point in the original motion. It concerned the question of provincehood for the Yukon territories. This seemed to be initially part of the motion which the hon. member was proposing. I have some quite strong reservations about provincehood for the Yukon or the Northwest Territories, not in the very long run but in the immediate short term. I believe that we should be aiming toward a constitutional mechanism which will allow the population of those two territories to have an efficient government. There should be a mechanism whereby they will be allowed to communicate and solve problems that are affected by directions from Ottawa. We should provide mechanisms which will allow a rapid and efficient flow-through, whenever Ottawa civil servants are involved, to the local population in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
We should get rid of the red tape, but we should consider the many alternatives before coming to the conclusion that provincehood for that size of population in these days is necessarily the only solution.
I would like to thank the hon. member for having given us the opportunity this afternoon to discuss this most important issue . I know that he is on the right track. This type of reconfirmation mechanism which he talks about is imaginative and, I believe, holds the key to the kind of reform in the Senate that will be meaningful, useful and effective as far as better government in Canada is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, in commenting on the proposition before us, I would say that while the New Democratic Party has long advocated the abolition of the Senate, that position should in no way be construed as signifying unalterable opposition to the concept of a second chamber if such a chamber were to be structured on a democratic, responsible and realistically representative foundation. Because of that long-held position which my party has taken, we as a party perhaps have not given the due measure of attention to the subject of alternatives that we otherwise would have done. Therefore, what I am about to say consists largely of my own musings on the subject, although they do arise from conversations with quite a large cross-section of people from different parts of the country with different economic and social backgrounds. They are in large part coloured by my own concept of what is one of my particular roles.
When I stood for election in 1980,1 was quite frank with my constituents. I told them that if they saw fit to elect me, they should be prepared for me to be somewhat of a shared representative. They elected me quite knowingly on that basis, not only as the representative of the geographical constituency of Kootenay West, which I am proud and honoured to represent, but as one of a very few blue collar industrial workers to have the good fortune or otherwise to be part of this place. As such, I and a very few other members of this House have a particular vantage point, which is somewhat different from that of others, to present on this subject and a number of others.
There are only half a dozen, if that, members of this House who can be called industrial wage earners. This is the inverted pyramid, as it is often called, where vast numbers of Canadians who earn their living by wages find themselves singularly unrepresented in terms of a government of people who do not share their background and experiences. That is an awkward position to be in from time to time.
Many of the values of that section of our population are not always reflected, shared or understood by people who come primarily from a middle-class background, the professions such as the legal profession or the old professions or from the academic community.
I mention this briefly because it strikes many of us that we feel no great excitement about the establishment of a second chamber which would repeat all of these errors in its type of selection, whether it be elected, appointed by region or otherwise. Such an institution will continue to see neglected the direct expressions, opinions and interests of a very large number of Canadians who, for a variety of reasons, have difficulty in being heard so as to ensure that their interests are adequately looked after by government at all levels. The nature of their work is something that prevents them from doing that.
If you ask any Canadian what he or she is, they will tell you that they are a Quebecer, a British Columbian, or a Manitoban. Very often they will give their specific region, province or place of origin. Second, they are likely to say they are either a carpenter, lawyer, secretary, woodworker, miner or teacher. In other words, whether people are elected or appointed, they are known by where they live or what they do.
Representation in this House is based largely on geographical borders and constituencies. They are largely artificial electoral areas. I am lucky because my constituency has natural frontiers that were recognized long before it was a constituency. Not all constituencies have that sense of homogeneity.
We do not represent parties as we are not elected on a proportional or party-list basis as in some other jurisdictions. We are elected geographically within regions.
There has been a lot of talk about divisions of opinions or interests in this country. All divisions are certainly not east and west, although they are the ones that make the headlines. Many of the serious divisions of a political and economic
June 4, 1982

nature are urban versus hinterland rather than east versus west. There are very common differences and attitudes between the interior of British Columbia and the lower mainland, including the major metropolis of Vancouver. The same is found in many areas of rural Alberta as opposed to the administrative and industrial centres of that province. It is found between northern Ontario and Toronto. There is probably no less love lost in those areas than between the east and the west of Canada. Very often what takes place within a province or region is just a microcosm of the divisions that take place on a broader scale. There are certainly many serious divisions between the hinterland of Quebec and Montreal and Quebec City. However, those distinctions are as representative of different geographic areas as they are of the different economic functions that a hinterland and an urban metropolis represent. It is basically a difference between the managerial and the consumer interests of a city and the interests of the producer population, particularly in the resource industries in the hinterland of our country, whether it is in relation to forestry, mining, agriculture or fishing.
While it is appropriate that a province choose representatives to sit in the Senate, I hope if a committee is formed to make choices as to what representatives shall sit in the second chamber, whether by election process or selection-which I suggest is probably more appropriate-by various provincial governments, I suggest there should be some requirement other than simply a moral one to ensure that within the selection process adequate weight is given to those economic interests which make up the various populations, whether on a regional basis within a province or of working people either independently or through their organizations.
Management groups also find themselves under-represented in this elected chamber, as do unions and employees. We are largely an academic, legal, professional institution, and business and labour find themselves almost totally excluded. That shows in the kinds of things we do, not only in terms of our social attitudes, our social legislation and many other aspects of legislation we draft, but it certainly also shows in the way we handle-rather, mishandle-our economy continuously as a government and as a Parliament.
What I am trying to say is that in my view and in the view of many other working Canadians-and a number of Canadians in the business community as well-the last thing we need in Canada is another middle-class institution with middle-class values and middle-class priorities. We have many institutions and many legislators who are basically woolly-headed idealists in the sense that if we simply pass a law they think we suddenly really change something. Most people in the work-a-day world, whether labour or management, realize that life, the constitutional process, the legislative process and the structure of our society, are largely like a long arm-wrestling contest. It is like two fish in a goldfish bowl. We go back and forth, and then end up somewhere in the middle. Thus we end up with packages or results which everyone, whether they love it or not,
Senate Reform
realize we have to live with, rather than engaging in a continuous infantile name calling in which no one accepts responsibility for anything. Perhaps I and a few of my colleagues who share my background are locked into our background in the sense that somehow we prefer a system in which, even if we are not absolutely satisfied with the outcome of a process of negotiations or bargaining, at some point we realize that the battle has to end; we sign our names, make our own commitments and put our names on the dotted line, and that is something we have to live with for x number of years. It does not happen that way here, and I really do not think we need another institution in which the same kind of unhealthy attitudes to life and the processes of living together continue to exist.
I suspect I am not in the enviable position of my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko), who has a specific formula in mind, although I am sure he is as flexible in this as he has been on other occasions and on other major subjects which have received quite a bit of consideration in this House in recent months and years. But if this proposal is to go ahead, either now or at some time in the future-and I am sure something akin to it will-I would like us to bear in mind that there is a large body of people out there in the country who feel left out of our processes. They do not look at this Parliament as really being their Parliament. They do not look at the courts of this land as really being their courts. They do not look at the Senate of this country as being their Senate. Sometimes they have a great deal of difficulty believing that the institutions to which we all pledge our loyalty really consider deeply what their legitimate interests are, quite apart from serving them. I hope in the drafting of any proposal for a second chamber we give consideration to other divisions, whether on a subregional or interest basis, to ensure that working people and people who have devoted their lives to participating in the productive aspects of our society, whether in labouring roles or in management roles, can say that it results in government not only "of the people, by the people and for the people", but also that they may have a vested stake in their institutions and they may exercise some continuing loyalty and ability to participate more directly in the decisions which affect their day to day lives.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in listening to what the previous speaker had to say about his perception that there is an under-representation in this House of working middle-class people. I really do not believe that because the vast majority of Canadians, by any reasonable definition, are middle class, and it may be that some hon. members in this chamber have gone on to university or have gone into academic life, but I think we will find that there is a large proportion of the members of this chamber who came from farming communities, who were farmers or who were the sons of farmers. 1 have an academic background, yes. I taught at the University of British Columbia. My father was an electrician, and I was raised in an electrician's family.

speechtext:
I have the same roots as the hon. member does. I was raised in the same kind of family. I lived with my parents for 23 years. My parents were middle-class people who had a labour union background, 43 years in the IBEW, and I rather resent it when the hon. member says that we are not middle class, that the working people are not represented in this chamber, that we do not know what the working people want, or that we do not have parents or relatives who are working people. I consider all Canadians to be working people. They just work in different ways.
With regard to the Senate and the reform of the Senate, there are a few things I would like to say. The time is very short, I realize, but I have been thinking about this, as has the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko), for some time, and I think the Senate needs to be reformed.
There are certan problems I see in the way the country is represented. I think we have difficulties with our political parties. All three political parties have expressed the feeling that the grass roots of political parties are not having enough input into what is going on here in Parliament, in the Senate, and generally in government at the federal, provincial and, indeed, at the municipal level to some extent as well.
There is also a definite and distinct problem with regional representation, and I think one of the major problems we have
faced in the last few years has been regional representation by federal-provincial conference, which bypasses Parliament and elected representatives. It is not acceptable, and we have to bring that regional representation in a very meaningful way back to this Parliament of Canada.
Finally, there is a problem of representation of political parties in different parts of the country. With respect to the proportional representation problem, it has been suggested that members of the House of Commons be elected in a certain way and that certain parts of the House be appointed on a proportional basis. I do not agree with that. I think we should all be elected by our people, but there could be another chamber where proportional representation would in fact be the case, and that could very well be the Senate.
I have some further ideas, but I see that our time has expired. I would like to put those ideas forward when this debate on the hon. member's motion resumes.
